questions.stemHtml: In uncontrolled diabetes, in which of the following cells there is decreased glucose uptake due to insulin deficiency:
questions.solution: Meta" data-dictid="b47c9c6144169277719010eaa1a0ee">insulin deficiency leads to decreased glucose uptake in cells that rely on insulin for glucose transport. Skeletal muscle cells are insulin-dependent, meaning they require insulin to facilitate the uptake of glucose via glucose transporters (e.g., GLUT4 ). In the absence of sufficient insulin, glucose uptake in skeletal muscle decreases, leading to elevated blood glucose levels. RBC (Option A) RBCs do not depend on insulin for glucose uptake. They use GLUT1 transporters, which allow glucose to enter the cells independently of insulin levels. Therefore, their glucose uptake is not significantly affected by insulin deficiency. Liver (Option C) The liver can take up glucose independently of insulin to some extent, especially under the influence of other hormones like glucagon. While insulin does regulate hepatic glucose uptake and production, the primary effect of insulin deficiency in the liver is increased glucose output (e.g., gluconeogenesis), not a significant decrease in uptake. Brain (Option D) Brain cells primarily use GLUT3 and GLUT1 transporters, which are insulin-independent. The brain can continue to take up glucose even in the absence of insulin. @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation: The eye on the side of the MLF lesion cannot turn inward (adduct) fully when attempting to look horizontally away from the lesion.

Horizontal Gaze Palsy (Option A ruled out)

  • Definition: Inability to voluntarily move both eyes beyond the midline in one horizontal direction.
  • Eye Movements:
    • Affected Side: Both eyes cannot look towards the involved side.
    • Unaffected Side: Gaze to the opposite side is typically normal.
    • Convergence: Usually preserved.
    • Oculocephalic Reflex: May overcome the palsy (if supranuclear lesion), indicating brainstem integrity.

Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia (INO) (Option B)

  • Definition: Lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF), disrupting horizontal gaze coordination.
  • Eye Movements:
    • Ipsilateral Eye (side of lesion): Impaired or slowed adduction (inward movement) when looking away from the lesion.
    • Contralateral Eye (opposite side): Abducting nystagmus (jerking outward movements).
    • Convergence: Crucially preserved.
    • Vertical Gaze: May be affected in bilateral cases.

3rd Nerve Palsy (Oculomotor Nerve Palsy) (Option C ruled out)

  • Definition: Dysfunction of the oculomotor nerve, controlling most eye movements and eyelid elevation.
  • Eye Movements (typically unilateral):
    • Resting Position: Eye is "down and out" (abducted and depressed).
    • Impaired Movements: Cannot adduct, elevate, or depress past the midline.
    • Pupil: Often dilated and unreactive (if parasympathetic fibers involved).
    • Ptosis: Drooping of the eyelid (partial or complete).

Myasthenia Gravis (Option D ruled out)

  • Definition: Autoimmune disorder causing fluctuating weakness of voluntary muscles, including ocular muscles.
  • Eye Movements (highly variable and fatiguing):
    • Ptosis: Common, often asymmetrical, fluctuates (worsens with fatigue, improves with rest).
    • Diplopia: Common, variable, affecting any direction of gaze, often changing.
    • Ophthalmoplegia: Weakness in any eye movement, non-localizing (doesn't fit a specific nerve palsy).
    • Fatigability: Eye movements worsen with sustained effort.
    • Pupils: Always normal.
    • Cogan's Lid Twitch: Brief overshoot of upper eyelid after downward gaze, followed by slow drop.

questions.stem: Which of the following nerves gives sensory supply to the orbit?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following nerves gives sensory supply to the orbit?
questions.solution: inal nerve (Cranial Nerve V) (Option B): This nerve is the primary sensory nerve for the face, including the orbit and its contents. Its ophthalmic division (V1) specifically provides sensory innervation to: The eye itself (cornea, conjunctiva, iris, ciliary body) The lacrimal gland The skin of the upper eyelid, forehead, and bridge of the nose Parts of the nasal cavity and sinuses. Let's look at why the other options are incorrect: Vagus nerve (Cranial Nerve X) (Option A ruled out) : Primarily involved in parasympathetic control of internal organs (heart, lungs, digestive system), and provides some sensory input from the ear and pharynx, but not the orbit. Hypoglossal nerve (Cranial Nerve XII) (Option C ruled out) : Purely a motor nerve that controls the muscles of the tongue. Oculomotor nerve (Cranial Nerve III) (Option D ruled out) : Primarily a motor nerve that controls most of the extraocular muscles (eye movements) and provides parasympathetic innervation to the pupil and ciliary muscle (for accommodation). It has very limited, if any, direct sensory supply to the orbit itself. @Neet_pg_bot

  • The lacrimal gland
  • The skin of the upper eyelid, forehead, and bridge of the nose

  • Risk factors for the formation of Renal Stones:

    Description

    Dietary factors

    • Hyperuricosuria (Option D)

      • Alkaline: Calcium phosphate stone formation

    Associated disorders

    • Inflammatory Bowel disease (IBD), especially Crohn’s Disease (calcium oxalate stones)
    • Gastric bypass surgery
    • Primary hyperparathyroidism (calcium oxalate stones)

    • Renal tubular acidosis Type 1 or distal (calcium phosphate stones)

questions.solution: rong> Meropenem is the most appropriate antibiotic for a diabetic patient in septic shock due to a complicated UTI, providing necessary broad-spectrum coverage, including for ESBL-producing organisms. In the given scenario, the patient with a complicated UTI and septic shock is most likely infected with Pseudomonas or Klebsiella, for which the drug of choice is meropenem, a Carbapenem antibiotic. questions.stem: A patient underwent cardiac surgery and was admitted to the ICU. He later developed ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and was started on empirical antibiotics. A few hours later, the patient developed acute kidney injury (AKI). Serum procalcitonin was sent. Which of the following statements regarding procalcitonin is correct?
questions.stemHtml: A patient underwent cardiac surgery and was admitted to the ICU. He later developed ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP) and was started on empirical antibiotics. A few hours later, the patient developed acute kidney injury (AKI). Serum procalcitonin was sent. Which of the following statements regarding procalcitonin is correct?

options.label: A
options.text: It helps in determining the duration of antibiotic therapy

options.label: B
options.text: It helps in identifying which empirical antibiotics to be given

options.label: C
options.text: It can be used to confirm source of infection

options.label: D
options.text: It is used to differentiate bacterial from fungal cause

questions.answerText: It helps in determining the duration of antibiotic therapy
questions.solution: g> Explanation: Procalcitonin (PCT) is widely used to guide the duration of antibiotic therapy , especially in ICU settings and conditions like ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). Serial PCT measurements help determine when to discontinue antibiotics , usually when PCT falls below 0.25–0.5 ng/mL or decreases by 80–90% from the peak value. Role of Procalcitonin: Helps detect bacterial infections early and differentiate from non-bacterial causes. Guides when to start or stop antibiotics based on specific cut-off values. Decreases by ~50% every 24 hours after infection control, helping monitor treatment. Differentiates between infectious and non-infectious conditions in various diseases. Reduces unnecessary antibiotic use in respiratory, postoperative, and other conditions. Correlates with severity in sepsis, offering prognostic information. Used in ED and ICU algorithms to manage antibiotic timing and duration. Levels <0.1 ng/mL have high negative predictive value to rule out bacterial infections. Incorrect Options: It helps in identifying which empirical antibiotics to be given (Option B): PCT does not identify specific pathogens or recommend particular antibiotics. It only indicates the likelihood of a bacterial infection, not which organisms are involved or their sensitivity patterns. Empirical antibiotic selection is based on clinical judgment, local antibiograms, and patient risk factors. It can be used to confirm source of infection (Option C): PCT is a non-specific marker of systemic bacterial infection and cannot pinpoint the source (e.g., lungs, urinary tract, blood). Imaging and cultures are needed to confirm the anatomical site of infection. It is used to differentiate bacterial from fungal cause (Option D): While PCT can help distinguish bacterial from viral infections, it is not reliable in differentiating bacterial from fungal infections. Invasive fungal infections may not always cause elevated PCT levels, limiting its utility in such cases. @Neet_pg_bot

Explanation:

  • Procalcitonin (PCT) is widely used to guide the duration of antibiotic therapy, especially in ICU settings and conditions like ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP). Serial PCT measurements help determine when to discontinue antibiotics, usually when PCT falls below 0.25–0.5 ng/mL or decreases by 80–90% from the peak value.

Role of Procalcitonin:

  • Helps detect bacterial infections early and differentiate from non-bacterial causes.
  • Guides when to start or stop antibiotics based on specific cut-off values.
  • Decreases by ~50% every 24 hours after infection control, helping monitor treatment.
  • Differentiates between infectious and non-infectious conditions in various diseases.
  • Reduces unnecessary antibiotic use in respiratory, postoperative, and other conditions.
  • Correlates with severity in sepsis, offering prognostic information.
  • Used in ED and ICU algorithms to manage antibiotic timing and duration.
  • Levels <0.1 ng/mL have high negative predictive value to rule out bacterial infections.

Incorrect Options:

It helps in identifying which empirical antibiotics to be given (Option B): PCT does not identify specific pathogens or recommend particular antibiotics. It only indicates the likelihood of a bacterial infection, not which organisms are involved or their sensitivity patterns. Empirical antibiotic selection is based on clinical judgment, local antibiograms, and patient risk factors.

It can be used to confirm source of infection (Option C): PCT is a non-specific marker of systemic bacterial infection and cannot pinpoint the source (e.g., lungs, urinary tract, blood). Imaging and cultures are needed to confirm the anatomical site of infection.

It is used to differentiate bacterial from fungal cause (Option D): While PCT can help distinguish bacterial from viral infections, it is not reliable in differentiating bacterial from fungal infections. Invasive fungal infections may not always cause elevated PCT levels, limiting its utility in such cases.

questions.stem: According to WHO, which of the following is the recommended diagnostic test for spinal tuberculosis?
questions.stemHtml: According to WHO, which of the following is the recommended diagnostic test for spinal tuberculosis?
questions.solution: ealth Organization (WHO), the recommended and definitive diagnostic test for spinal tuberculosis is Culture and Sensitivity. Spinal tuberculosis, also known as Pott’s disease, is a form of extrapulmonary TB that primarily affects the vertebral column. Diagnosing spinal TB is more complex than pulmonary TB because it typically involves deeper tissues and presents with nonspecific symptoms like chronic back pain, fever, weight loss, and neurological deficits in advanced stages. WHO strongly recommends CB-NAAT as a first-line test for extrapulmonary TB , including spinal TB, because it gives results within hours and helps initiate treatment quickly. However, due to its certain limitations, it cannot replace culture as the definitive test. (Option C) Imaging used for diagnosing Pott’s spine: MRI: Investigation of choice to evaluate the type and extent of compression of the cord. IOC for potts spine and potts paraplegia. But doesn't help to visualize bony vertebral destruction. Earlier signs, spinal nerve root, and paraspinal soft tissue are better visualized. The best diagnostic modality for spinal TB. CT scan: (Option B) The most preferred imaging modality for the assessment of destruction of the vertebral body and sequestrum formation. The pattern of bone damage, including fragmentary, osteolytic, sclerotic, and subperiosteal changes, is clearly visible on CT scans. X-ray: (Option A) is useful as an initial imaging tool, but it lacks sensitivity and may miss early disease. Findings are: Reduction of disc space- Lateral X-ray is better for the evaluation of disc space. In the early stages- wedging of the vertebrae. In late stages- angular kyphotic deformity . Evidence of cold abscess: Bird nest appearance of cold abscess of the thoracic region showing typical fusiform shape. Rarefaction: There is diffuse rarefaction of the vertebrae above and below the lesion. Types of lesions in the vertebral column are: Paradiscal (most common) Central Anterior Posterior ( pedicle, lamina, spinous process, and transverse process) Signs of healing: Sclerosis Sclerotic bone Bony fusion @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: id="1e4db8b6ad1692777183683f42d44b">Brachial Index < 0.3 indicates an imminently threatened leg and requires urgent vascular assessment/revascularisation to prevent major amputation. Chronic Limb Threatening Ischemia (CLTI) is defined as rest pain or tissue loss (ulcers, or gangrene) supported by ischemia defined by the hemodynamic criteria of low ankle or toe pressures, or low transcutaneous oxygen (TcO2) values. Ankle pressure criteria range from less than 40–70mmHg, toe pressures less than 30–50mmHg, TcO2 less than 20–40mmHg. CLTI is assessed by measuring Ankle Brachial Pressure Index or Ankle Brachial Index (ABPI/ABI). ABPI is measured supine by checking the systolic blood pressure in both upper and lower limbs (brachial, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis arteries). The higher value from each limb is used to calculate the ABPI. This index is calculated as: ABI = Systolic BP in the Ankle/ Systolic BP in the arm Interpretations are as follows: Value Interpretation 0.1 - 0.4 Critical limb ischemia 0.5 - 0.9 Intermittent claudication 1.0 - 1.2 Normal > 1.2 Calcified vessels (seen in patients with DM, End stage renal disease) @Neet_pg_bot

Most affected by outliers: Mean The best measure of central tendency in skewed observations: Median The least affected measure: Mode Measures of Dispersion (Option B) : Measures Definition Calculation Standard deviation Measures the variation or dispersion of a set of values around the mean. σ = √(∑(x− x̄) 2 /n) Range The difference between the highest and lowest values in a dataset. Range = Maximum value - Minimum value Mean deviation Measures the average absolute deviation of data points from the mean. Mean deviation = ∑ X - x̄ / n Variance Measures the average of the squared differences from the mean. Variance = σ 2 Measures of correlation (Option D) show how two variables relate, indicating the strength and direction of their association. Pearson’s coefficient (r) ranges from -1 to +1, with values near 0 showing no linear relationship. questions.solution: > Explanation: Lumbar Puncture is contraindicated in patients with Platelet count below 50,000 (plts)/μLas it carries a high risk of spinal/epidural hematoma. (Option D) Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) is a well-known complication of LP, more common in young adults , especially females. (Option A) It occurs due to CSF leak following a puncture of the dura mater in procedures involving spinal anesthesia, epidural catheter placement. Meningitis after LP is rare if aseptic technique is followed, hence this statement is correct. (Option B) Introducing a needle into an infected area carries a high risk of spreading the infection to the spinal canal, potentially leading to meningitis or epidural abscess. In suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) the first-line investigation is non-contrast CT (NCCT) of the head and sometimes NCCT can show normal findings. In such cases, LP is mandatory to confirm or rule out SAH, to look for Xanthochromia (yellow discoloration due to breakdown of RBCs) in the CSF. (Option C) Indications of Lumbar Puncture: Meningitis Encephalitis Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) Suspicion of nervous system diseases (like Guillain-Barré syndrome and carcinomatous meningitis) Therapeutic relief of pseudotumor cerebri Encephalitis Dementia Myelitis Leukemia Autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis Contraindications of Lumbar Puncture: Absolute Contraindications Relative Contraindications Presence of infected skin or cellulitis at the site of needle insertion. Evidence of unequal intracranial pressures between the supratentorial and infratentorial compartments Increased ICP Coagulopathy or bleeding disorders Brain abscess @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
>

Explanation:

  • Lumbar Puncture is contraindicated in patients with Platelet count below 50,000 (plts)/μLas it carries a high risk of spinal/epidural hematoma. (Option D)
  • Post-dural puncture headache (PDPH) is a well-known complication of LP, more common in young adults, especially females. (Option A)
    • It occurs due to CSF leak following a puncture of the dura mater in procedures involving spinal anesthesia, epidural catheter placement.
  • Meningitis after LP is rare if aseptic technique is followed, hence this statement is correct. (Option B)
    • Introducing a needle into an infected area carries a high risk of spreading the infection to the spinal canal, potentially leading to meningitis or epidural abscess.
  • In suspected subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH) the first-line investigation is non-contrast CT (NCCT) of the head and sometimes NCCT can show normal findings.
    • In such cases, LP is mandatory to confirm or rule out SAH, to look for Xanthochromia (yellow discoloration due to breakdown of RBCs) in the CSF. (Option C)
       

Indications of Lumbar Puncture:

  • Meningitis
  • Encephalitis
  • Subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH)
  • Suspicion of nervous system diseases (like Guillain-Barré syndrome and carcinomatous meningitis)
  • Therapeutic relief of pseudotumor cerebri
  • Encephalitis
  • Dementia
  • Myelitis
  • Leukemia
  • Autoimmune diseases such as multiple sclerosis

Contraindications of Lumbar Puncture:

Absolute Contraindications

Relative Contraindications
  • Presence of infected skin or cellulitis at the site of needle insertion.
  • Evidence of unequal intracranial pressures between the supratentorial and infratentorial compartments
  • Increased ICP
  • Coagulopathy or bleeding disorders
  • Brain abscess

questions.solution: : The gene pool consists of all copies of every type of allele at every locus in all members of the population. This definition emphasizes that the gene pool encompasses genetic variation across an entire population, not just an individual or family. Family (Option A) A family represents only a small subset of a population and does not encompass all genetic diversity. Individual (Option B) An individual has only two alleles per gene (diploid), not the entire pool of alleles. Tissue (Option D) Tissue is a group of cells that have similar structure and that function together as a unit. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A male presents with lesions and a history of unprotected sexual intercourse a few months ago. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A male presents with lesions and a history of unprotected sexual intercourse a few months ago. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.solution: ong> The lesions depicted in the image, along with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse, suggest a diagnosis of Secondary Syphilis , which is best confirmed through serological testing. It is the second stage of syphilis, which occurs if primary syphilis is left untreated. It presents a few weeks to several months after the initial chancre has healed. It is marked by systemic manifestations and can affect multiple organ systems. Clinical Features: Diffuse, non-pruritic rash, often reddish-brown macules or papules, that is polymorphous and non-vesicular . Mucous membrane lesions, such as condylomata lata , appear in moist areas like the oral cavity and genitals and are highly infectious. Oral signs may include mucous patches or snail track ulcers. “Moth-eaten" alopecia : A patchy, non-scarring hair loss. Buschke-Ollendorff sign : Deep tenderness over lesions. Painless generalized lymphadenopathy (especially epitrochlear nodes)l. Systemic symptoms include fever, malaise, and fatigue, with rare cases showing neurological or ocular involvement. Diagnosis : By serological testing: (Option A) Non-Treponemal Tests : RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) and VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) are used for screening. These tests detect nonspecific antibodies and can be positive in other conditions. Treponemal Tests : FTA-ABS (Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption) confirms the diagnosis by detecting antibodies specific to Treponema pallidum. Treatment: Standard treatment: Benzathine penicillin G . Dosage: 2.4 million units intramuscularly in a single dose. For those allergic to penicillin, alternatives such as doxycycline or tetracycline can be used. Complications : If left untreated, secondary syphilis can progress to the latent stage and eventually tertiary syphilis, which can lead to serious complications, including cardiovascular, neurological, and systemic damage. Tzanck smear (Option B) is a diagnostic test primarily used for identifying infections caused by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella-Zoster Virus. It involves examining cells scraped from a lesion under a microscope. However, this test has no role in diagnosing syphilis, as it does not detect Treponema pallidum, the bacterium responsible for the disease. KOH preparation (Option C) is commonly employed to diagnose superficial fungal infections such as dermatophytosis or candidiasis. A sample from the skin, hair, or nails is treated with potassium hydroxide, which dissolves keratin and allows for the visualization of fungal elements under a microscope. Since syphilis is a bacterial infection, this test is irrelevant in its diagnosis. Biopsy (Option D) is used to evaluate suspicious skin lesions when the diagnosis is unclear, and it can sometimes reveal histopathological features suggestive of syphilis. The lesions depicted in the image, along with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse, suggest a diagnosis of Secondary Syphilis, which is best confirmed through serological testing.

  • It is the second stage of syphilis, which occurs if primary syphilis is left untreated.
  • It presents a few weeks to several months after the initial chancre has healed.
  • It is marked by systemic manifestations and can affect multiple organ systems.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Diffuse, non-pruritic rash, often reddish-brown macules or papules, that is polymorphous and non-vesicular.
    • Mucous membrane lesions, such as condylomata lata, appear in moist areas like the oral cavity and genitals and are highly infectious.
    • Oral signs may include mucous patches or snail track ulcers.
    • “Moth-eaten" alopecia: A patchy, non-scarring hair loss.
    • Buschke-Ollendorff sign: Deep tenderness over lesions.
    • Painless generalized lymphadenopathy (especially epitrochlear nodes)l.
    • Systemic symptoms include fever, malaise, and fatigue, with rare cases showing neurological or ocular involvement.
  • Diagnosis: By serological testing: (Option A)
    • Non-Treponemal Tests:
      • RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) and VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) are used for screening.
      • These tests detect nonspecific antibodies and can be positive in other conditions.
    • Treponemal Tests:
      • FTA-ABS (Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption) confirms the diagnosis by detecting antibodies specific to Treponema pallidum.
  • Treatment:
    • Standard treatment: Benzathine penicillin G.
    • Dosage: 2.4 million units intramuscularly in a single dose.
    • For those allergic to penicillin, alternatives such as doxycycline or tetracycline can be used.
  • Complications: If left untreated, secondary syphilis can progress to the latent stage and eventually tertiary syphilis, which can lead to serious complications, including cardiovascular, neurological, and systemic damage.

Tzanck smear (Option B) is a diagnostic test primarily used for identifying infections caused by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella-Zoster Virus. It involves examining cells scraped from a lesion under a microscope. However, this test has no role in diagnosing syphilis, as it does not detect Treponema pallidum, the bacterium responsible for the disease.

KOH preparation (Option C) is commonly employed to diagnose superficial fungal infections such as dermatophytosis or candidiasis. A sample from the skin, hair, or nails is treated with potassium hydroxide, which dissolves keratin and allows for the visualization of fungal elements under a microscope. Since syphilis is a bacterial infection, this test is irrelevant in its diagnosis.


Biopsy (Option D) is used to evaluate suspicious skin lesions when the diagnosis is unclear, and it can sometimes reveal histopathological features suggestive of syphilis. It is invasive and nonspecific, whereas serological tests are more sensitive, specific, and the preferred method for diagnosing secondary syphilis.

questions.stem: A patient develops ataxia while taking carbamazepine and erythromycin. What is the most likely cause?
questions.stemHtml: A patient develops ataxia while taking carbamazepine and erythromycin. What is the most likely cause?
questions.solution: enzyme that metabolizes Carbamazepine , leading to elevated carbamazepine levels and resulting in toxicity, with ataxia being a common symptom. MOA: Inhibits high-frequency neuronal discharges and modulates voltage-gated sodium channels. Uses: Trigeminal neuralgia GTCS (generalized tonic clonic seizures) Partial seizures Bipolar disorder. Interactions: Metabolism of carbamazepine is induced by phenobarbitone, phenytoin, and vice versa. Erythromycin, fluoxetine, and isoniazid inhibit the metabolism of carbamazepine. (Option A) Adverse Effects Description Neurotoxicity Sedation, dizziness, vertigo, diplopia, and ataxia Gastrointestinal Effects Vomiting and diarrhoea occur with higher doses. Acute Intoxication Coma, convulsions, cardiovascular collapse. Haematological Agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia. Hypersensitivity Reactions Rashes, photosensitivity, hepatitis, lupus-like syndrome. Water Retention and Hyponatremia Due to enhanced antidiuretic hormone (ADH) action, it is more common in the elderly. Teratogenicity Increased incidence of minor fetal malformations. Erythromycin toxicity (Option B) is not the cause, as it rarely causes ataxia. Its main role here is as a CYP3A4 inhibitor, which increases carbamazepine levels and leads to toxicity. Worsening of the underlying disease (Option C) can cause ataxia, but the timing after starting erythromycin points to a drug interaction, making this less likely. A separate, unrelated neurological condition (Option D) is unlikely, as the timing with carbamazepine and erythromycin use suggests a drug interaction rather than a new, unrelated diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot

enzyme that metabolizes Carbamazepine, leading to elevated carbamazepine levels and resulting in toxicity, with ataxia being a common symptom.
  • MOA: Inhibits high-frequency neuronal discharges and modulates voltage-gated sodium channels.
  • Uses:
    • Trigeminal neuralgia
    • GTCS (generalized tonic clonic seizures)
    • Partial seizures
    • Bipolar disorder.
  • Interactions:
    • Metabolism of carbamazepine is induced by phenobarbitone, phenytoin, and vice versa.
    • Erythromycin, fluoxetine, and isoniazid inhibit the metabolism of carbamazepine. (Option A)

 

Adverse Effects

Description

Neurotoxicity

Sedation, dizziness, vertigo, diplopia, and ataxia

Gastrointestinal Effects

Vomiting and diarrhoea occur with higher doses.

Acute Intoxication

Coma, convulsions, cardiovascular collapse.

Haematological

Agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia.

Hypersensitivity Reactions

Rashes, photosensitivity, hepatitis, lupus-like syndrome.

Water Retention and Hyponatremia

Due to enhanced antidiuretic hormone (ADH) action, it is more common in the elderly.

Teratogenicity

Increased incidence of minor fetal malformations.

Erythromycin toxicity (Option B) is not the cause, as it rarely causes ataxia. Its main role here is as a CYP3A4 inhibitor, which increases carbamazepine levels and leads to toxicity.

Worsening of the underlying disease (Option C) can cause ataxia, but the timing after starting erythromycin points to a drug interaction, making this less likely.

A separate, unrelated neurological condition (Option D) is unlikely, as the timing with carbamazepine and erythromycin use suggests a drug interaction rather than a new, unrelated diagnosis.

questions.solution: dictid="e24b7bd55d16927771818aaa6ad0ed">anesthesia to diagnose Explanation: Recurrent epistaxis (Option A ruled out): This is a hallmark symptom of JNA. These tumors are highly vascular, leading to frequent and often heavy nosebleeds. So, this is seen in JNA. Unilateral nasal obstruction (Option B ruled out): This is also a very common symptom as the tumor grows and fills the nasopharynx and nasal cavity. So, this is seen in JNA. Exclusively to adolescent boys (Option C ruled out): JNA primarily and overwhelmingly affects adolescent boys . While very rare cases in younger children or post-adolescent males (up to early 20s) have been reported, it is virtually unheard of in females and is a defining characteristic of the disease. So, this statement is largely true, implying it's a key feature. Biopsy under anesthesia to diagnose(Option D): This is the correct answer; this is NOT typically done for JNA . JNA is a highly vascular tumor. Performing a biopsy carries a significant risk of severe, life-threatening hemorrhage. Diagnosis is usually made based on characteristic clinical presentation (recurrent epistaxis, unilateral nasal obstruction in an adolescent boy) and, most importantly, characteristic imaging findings (CT and MRI). If a biopsy is considered absolutely necessary for an atypical presentation, it is performed in a controlled environment like an operating room where bleeding can be immediately managed, often after preoperative embolization to reduce blood supply to the tumor. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: The Kanagawa phenomenon observed on Wagatsuma agar is characteristic of which of the following organisms?
questions.stemHtml: The Kanagawa phenomenon observed on Wagatsuma agar is characteristic of which of the following organisms?
questions.solution: parahaemolyticus Explanation: The Kanagawa phenomenon refers to β-hemolysis (clear zone of hemolysis) produced by Vibrio parahaemolyticus on Wagatsuma agar (a type of high salt blood agar). It is an enteropathogenic halophilic vibrio. Food-borne gastroenteritis (most common) occurs following raw or uncooked sea food intake. Features: It grows only in media containing NaCl. TCBS agar : Green colonies with an opaque, raised centre and flat translucent periphery. String test: Positive. It is oxidase, catalase, nitrate, indole and citrate positive. Antigenic components: Somatic 0, capsular K and flagellar H antigens. Shows Kanagawa phenomenon on wagatsuma agar Microscopy: Bipolar safety pin appearance Vibrio cholerae (Option A) is a Gram-negative, comma-shaped bacterium that causes cholera, a diarrheal illness often associated with contaminated water. It does not show this hemolysis pattern and is not associated with the characteristic reactions on Wagatsuma agar. Staphylococcus aureus (Option C) , a Gram-positive cocci often found in clusters, is responsible for skin abscesses, toxic shock syndrome. While it can cause β-hemolysis on blood agar, it is not associated with the Kanagawa phenomenon. Burkholderia pseudomallei (Option D) is a Gram-negative rod that causes melioidosis. It primarily affects individuals with underlying conditions, such as diabetes. It does not grow on Wagatsuma agar, nor does it exhibit the Kanagawa phenomenon. @Neet_pg_bot

parahaemolyticus

Explanation:

The Kanagawa phenomenon refers to β-hemolysis (clear zone of hemolysis) produced by Vibrio parahaemolyticus on Wagatsuma agar (a type of high salt blood agar).

  • It is an enteropathogenic halophilic vibrio.
  • Food-borne gastroenteritis (most common) occurs following raw or uncooked sea food intake.
  • Features:
    • It grows only in media containing NaCl.
    • TCBS agar: Green colonies with an opaque, raised centre and flat translucent periphery.
    • String test: Positive.
    • It is oxidase, catalase, nitrate, indole and citrate positive.
    • Antigenic components: Somatic 0, capsular K and flagellar H antigens.
    • Shows Kanagawa phenomenon on wagatsuma agar
    • Microscopy: Bipolar safety pin appearance

Vibrio cholerae (Option A) is a Gram-negative, comma-shaped bacterium that causes cholera, a diarrheal illness often associated with contaminated water. It does not show this hemolysis pattern and is not associated with the characteristic reactions on Wagatsuma agar.

Staphylococcus aureus (Option C), a Gram-positive cocci often found in clusters, is responsible for skin abscesses, toxic shock syndrome. While it can cause β-hemolysis on blood agar, it is not associated with the Kanagawa phenomenon.


Burkholderia pseudomallei (Option D) is a Gram-negative rod that causes melioidosis. It primarily affects individuals with underlying conditions, such as diabetes. It does not grow on Wagatsuma agar, nor does it exhibit the Kanagawa phenomenon.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old female sustained an Intertrochanteric Fracture. Which of the following is the Best Management?
questions.stemHtml: A 78-year-old female sustained an Intertrochanteric Fracture. Which of the following is the Best Management?
questions.solution: p> Explanation: Proximal Femoral Nail (intramedullary fixation) is the treatment of choice for most intertrochanteric fractures, especially unstable patterns , which are common in the elderly. Its is a fracture between the greater and lesser trochanters may lead to slight disruption of Shenton's line due to misalignment, often less pronounced than neck fractures. It is almost always managed by internal fixation with implants (e.g., dynamic hip screws, intramedullary nails) The Proximal Femoral Nail (PFN) is used for closed intramedullary fixation of proximal femoral fractures. It features two proximal openings for a femoral neck lag screw and an anti-rotation screw. Indications include peritrochanteric, intertrochanteric, and subtrochanteric fractures. It is contraindicated for medial femoral neck fractures. Aspect Intertrochanteric Fracture Location Extracapsular (outside the joint capsule) Age Group Typically after 60 years Sex Male > Female Common Patient Demographics Elderly (low-energy trauma); rare high-energy trauma in younger patients Mechanism of Injury Low-energy trauma in elderly; usually requires significant trauma in younger patients Stability Generally unstable due to muscle forces and location Ability to Walk Walking is not possible due to the instability Blood Loss More blood loss, due to the involvement of surrounding vascular structures Pain, Severity, and Tenderness Severe pain, more generalized around the hip with marked tenderness over the greater trochanter. Weight-bearing is difficult or impossible. Complications Malunion is more common than nonunion Internal Fixation with Screws (Option B) is better suitable for femoral neck fractures , not intertrochanteric fractures as it does not provide sufficient stability in osteoporotic bone. Prosthetic Replacement (Option C) is done in femoral neck fractures , especially when there's risk of avascular necrosis or poor healing . It is not typically used for intertrochanteric fractures unless there's severe comminution or failed fixation, and in elderly with osteoporosis. Boot & Traction (Option D) was previously used for temporary alignment and pain relief . It does not provide fracture stability or promote healing, it's not definitive treatment . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A woman with a history of proliferative diabetic retinopathy presents with gradual vision changes in her right eye. She reports seeing floaters and flashes of light. What type of retinal detachment is most likely in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A woman with a history of proliferative diabetic retinopathy presents with gradual vision changes in her right eye. She reports seeing floaters and flashes of light. What type of retinal detachment is most likely in this patient?
questions.solution: -dictid="a5603ff98316927771865d7ae41f16">diabetic woman with proliferative retinopathy with gradual visual loss is most likely to be due to Tractional Retinal Detachment. Retinal detachment refers to the separation of the neurosensory retina from the retinal pigment epithelium. Retinal detachment can be classified into three types: Rhegmatogenous or primary retinal detachment Tractional retinal detachment Exudative retinal detachment Rhegmatogenous Retinal Detachment : This is the most common type and occurs due to a retinal tear or break, allowing subretinal fluid to enter and separate the sensory retina from the pigmentary epithelium. Tractional Retinal Detachment : Results from the pulling of the retina by fibrous or vascular tissue, commonly seen in fibrovascular proliferative conditions like diabetic retinopathy, without a retinal break. questions.stem: The contraction phase of a single muscle twitch lasts 40 milliseconds. What is the tetanization frequency required to produce a sustained contraction in this muscle?
questions.stemHtml: The contraction phase of a single muscle twitch lasts 40 milliseconds. What is the tetanization frequency required to produce a sustained contraction in this muscle?
questions.solution: /strong> Tetanization occurs when successive muscle twitches summate to produce a sustained contraction, meaning the muscle doesn't have time to fully relax between stimuli. For this to happen, the frequency of stimulation must be high enough that the next stimulus arrives before the muscle twitch from the previous stimulus has completely relaxed. If the contraction phase of a single muscle twitch lasts 40 milliseconds (ms), then to achieve summation and eventually tetanus, the stimuli must be delivered at intervals shorter than or equal to this relaxation time. The frequency (Hz) is the reciprocal of the time period (in seconds). Time period (T) = 40 ms = 0.040 seconds Frequency (f) = 1 / T = 1 / 0.040 Hz Frequency (f) = 25 Hz Therefore, a frequency of 25 Hz or higher would be required to produce a sustained contraction (tetanus) in this muscle. @Neet_pg_bot

Increased frequency of micturition (cystitis) Lab investigations: Urine: Turbid, contains pus cells and bacteria Toxemia (acute pyelonephritis) Raised blood urea and casts present Treatement Keep the patient in bed, lying on the unaffected side (prevent pressure upon the tender renal angle). Explanation:

In a 29-year-old woman in her first trimester with asymptomatic bacteriuria caused by E. coli, the most common complication if left untreated is Pyelonephritis (Pyelitis).

  • It is an infection of the upper urinary tract involving the kidneys,
  • It is mostly a complication of the lower urinary tract involving infections.
    • Infections of postoperative and puerperal cystitis often spread to the kidneys to cause pyelonephritis.
  • In pregnancy, the infective organism is usually E. coli. (Option C)
  • Ascending pyelonephritis: Complication of advanced carcinoma of the cervix and vagina.
  • Recurrent attacks: Occur in patients who have had ureterocolic transplantation
  • Clinical features
    • Pain and tenderness in the loin
      • Acute pyelonephritis: Affected kidney region is exquisitely tender
      • Chronic pyelonephritis: Tenderness and rigidity along the course of the ureter
    • High temperature
    • Frequent rigors, headache, vomiting, and furring of the tongue.
    • Increased frequency of micturition (cystitis)
  • Lab investigations:
    • Urine: Turbid, contains pus cells and bacteria
    • Toxemia (acute pyelonephritis)
      • Raised blood urea and casts present
  • Treatement
    • Keep the patient in bed, lying on the unaffected side (prevent pressure upon the tender renal angle).
    • Copious fluid administration
    • Systemic antibiotics, followed by oral fluid, for 10-14 days
    • Referral to urologist, if no response.

Incorrect Options:

Chorioamnionitis (Option A) is an infection of the fetal membranes, usually linked to prolonged rupture of membranes or invasive procedures. It is not directly associated with asymptomatic bacteriuria, making it an unlikely complication in this case.

Preterm labor (Option B) may result from untreated UTIs like pyelonephritis but is a secondary complication. The main concern with asymptomatic bacteriuria is its progression to pyelonephritis.

Low birth weight (Option D) can result from maternal infections like pyelonephritis but is not a direct or early complication of asymptomatic bacteriuria. It may occur later due to chronic infection affecting fetal growth.

questions.stem: A 4 year old boy was suffering ear infection and tonic spasms of limbs, with fever and neck rigidity. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 4 year old boy was suffering ear infection and tonic spasms of limbs, with fever and neck rigidity. Which of the following is the likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Meningitis (Option A): The classic triad of symptoms for meningitis includes fever, neck rigidity (nuchal rigidity), and altered mental status or seizures (like tonic spasms) . An ear infection is a well-known risk factor for bacterial meningitis, especially in children, where bacteria from the ear can spread to the meninges. This combination of symptoms is a medical emergency. Bezold's Abscess (Option B ruled out): While a complication of an ear infection, Bezold's abscess primarily presents with pain and swelling in the neck, associated with mastoiditis. It does not directly cause neck rigidity or tonic spasms as primary symptoms. These neurological symptoms would only occur if the Bezold's abscess led to a further complication like meningitis. Sigmoid Sinus Thrombophlebitis (Option C ruled out): This is an intracranial complication of ear infection. It can cause fever and headache, and in severe cases, neurological deficits including seizures. However, neck rigidity is not a primary or consistent feature of sigmoid sinus thrombophlebitis itself. While it could potentially complicate into meningitis, making meningitis the more direct cause of the current full symptom set. Tetanus (Option D ruled out): As discussed previously, tetanus is caused by a bacterial toxin from a wound, not an ear infection. While it causes severe muscle spasms and rigidity, the etiology (ear infection) and the specific presentation (fever and neck rigidity along with spasms) do not fit tetanus. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: 27771957d22da5a71">perianal itching that worsens at night, is characteristic of an Enterobius vermicularis (Pinworm/Threadworm) infection. Epidemiology: The most common age group are school children . Infections can persist for years due to auto-infective cycles . Factors contributing to infection include: Overcrowding Impaired hygiene Poor personal care practices (such as nail-biting and inadequate handwashing). Morphology Adult worm The adults are short, white, and fusiform, resembling bits of white thread. The mouth is surrounded by three wing-like structures called cervical alae, which are transversely striated. Female worm Females are long. The posterior third tapers into a thin, pointed, pin-like tail. Females are oviparous. Male worm The posterior end is tightly curved ventrally, sharply truncated, and has a prominent copulatory spicule. Eggs The eggs are colorless and not bile-stained They float in saturated salt solution and have an elongated ovoid shape. Each egg contains a tadpole-shaped, coiled embryo that becomes infectious only 6 hours after being deposited . Life cycle Scotch-tape test: A piece of clear tape is pressed against the skin around the anus to collect eggs, typically overnight. The tape is then examined under a microscope for pinworm eggs. Hookworms (Option C) , including Ancylostoma duodenale (Option B) and Necator americanus, infect through skin penetration and migrate to the intestines, where they feed on blood and may cause iron-deficiency anemia. It can cause mild gastrointestinal symptoms like abdominal discomfort or diarrhea, but perianal itching is not a typical symptom. Eggs are diagnosed via stool microscopy, and the scotch tape test is not used for its detection. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 65-year-old patient is on mechanical ventilation for acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Suddenly, the patient becomes hypotensive, tachycardic, and shows absent breath sounds on the left side with tracheal deviation to the right. What is the most common cause of this in patients receiving mechanical ventilation?

options.label: B
options.text: Barotrauma due to high airway pressure

questions.answerText: Barotrauma due to high airway pressure
questions.solution: 80b697887ccb">airway pressure Explanation: Patients with ARDS often require high airway pressures during mechanical ventilation to maintain oxygenation. This increases the risk of barotrauma , leads to alveolar rupture and air leakage into extra-alveolar spaces , causing complications such as pneumothorax, pneumomediastinum , or subcutaneous emphysema . Ventilator factors that increase the risk: High plateau pressure (>30–35 cm H₂O) High peak inspiratory pressures High tidal volumes Auto-PEEP from inadequate exhalation Prevention: Plateau pressure is limited to ≤30 cm H₂O to minimize the risk of barotrauma and pneumothorax. High tidal volume (Option A) can contribute to barotrauma but they are not the direct cause of sudden hemodynamic collapse and tracheal deviation. Endotracheal tube malposition (Option C) usually leads to unilateral ventilation (e.g., right main bronchus intubation), causing decreased breath sounds on the left but it does not explain the tracheal shift or hemodynamic instability. Oxygen toxicity (Option D) develops gradually over prolonged exposure to high FiO₂ in ARDS. It does not cause sudden collapse or tracheal deviation. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Ventilator factors that increase the risk:

    • High peak inspiratory pressures
    • High tidal volumes

Endotracheal tube malposition (Option C) usually leads to unilateral ventilation (e.g., right main bronchus intubation), causing decreased breath sounds on the left but it does not explain the tracheal shift or hemodynamic instability.

Oxygen toxicity (Option D) develops gradually over prolonged exposure to high FiO₂ in ARDS. It does not cause sudden collapse or tracheal deviation.

questions.stem: According to the Muir-Barclay formula, which of the following is considered the best colloid for volume replacement?
questions.stemHtml: According to the Muir-Barclay formula, which of the following is considered the best colloid for volume replacement?
questions.solution: > The Muir-Barclay formula is used to calculate fluid and colloid replacement, especially in burns and trauma, and it emphasizes colloid volume efficiency. Among various colloids, Albumin is preferred because of its: High oncotic pressure Longer intravascular half-life Efficient plasma volume expansion Lower risk of allergic reactions compared to synthetic colloids like Dextran Muir and Barclay regime calculates the colloid fluid volume specifically. Muir and Barclay regime: For colloid after 12-24 hours ½ (% Burns x Body weight in kg) = 1 Ration 3 Rations in the first 12 hours 2 Rations in the second 12 hours 1 Ration in the third 12 hours Fluid resuscitation in burns: Fluid Management in the First 24 Hours Only crystalloids should be given (e.g., saline, dextrose saline, Ringer lactate-fluid of choice) Fluid Management After 24 Hours (Up to 30-48 Hours) Colloids should be given to compensate for plasma loss (Plasma, Haemaccel (gelatin), Dextrans, Hetastarch) Human albumin is considered the ideal colloid Blood is transfused later (after 48 hours) Incorrect Options: Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBC) (Option A): PRBCs are used to restore oxygen-carrying capacity, not primarily for volume replacement. They are not colloids for volume expansion. Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) (Option B): FFP is used for replacing clotting factors, especially in coagulopathies. It’s not primarily used as a volume expander and poses risks like allergic reactions or transfusion-related lung injury. Dextran 40 (Option C): Dextran is a synthetic colloid that can expand plasma volume, but it carries higher risks of Anaphylactic reactions, Coagulopathy and Renal impairment. Hence, it is not considered the best colloid for volume replacement. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
>

The Muir-Barclay formula is used to calculate fluid and colloid replacement, especially in burns and trauma, and it emphasizes colloid volume efficiency. Among various colloids, Albumin is preferred because of its:

  • High oncotic pressure
  • Longer intravascular half-life
  • Efficient plasma volume expansion
  • Lower risk of allergic reactions compared to synthetic colloids like Dextran

Muir and Barclay regime calculates the colloid fluid volume specifically.

Muir and Barclay regime: For colloid after 12-24 hours

  • ½ (% Burns x Body weight in kg) = 1 Ration
    • 3 Rations in the first 12 hours
    • 2 Rations in the second 12 hours
    • 1 Ration in the third 12 hours

Fluid resuscitation in burns:

  • Fluid Management in the First 24 Hours
    • Only crystalloids should be given (e.g., saline, dextrose saline, Ringer lactate-fluid of choice)
  • Fluid Management After 24 Hours (Up to 30-48 Hours)
    • Colloids should be given to compensate for plasma loss (Plasma, Haemaccel (gelatin), Dextrans, Hetastarch)
    • Human albumin is considered the ideal colloid
  • Blood is transfused later (after 48 hours)

Incorrect Options:

Packed Red Blood Cells (PRBC) (Option A): PRBCs are used to restore oxygen-carrying capacity, not primarily for volume replacement. They are not colloids for volume expansion.

Fresh Frozen Plasma (FFP) (Option B): FFP is used for replacing clotting factors, especially in coagulopathies. It’s not primarily used as a volume expander and poses risks like allergic reactions or transfusion-related lung injury.

Dextran 40 (Option C): Dextran is a synthetic colloid that can expand plasma volume, but it carries higher risks of Anaphylactic reactions, Coagulopathy and Renal impairment. Hence, it is not considered the best colloid for volume replacement.

questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old male presents to the emergency department with severe respiratory distress, BP: 70/59 mmHg, tracheal deviation to the right, distended neck veins, and absent breath sounds on the left side. These findings are suggestive of a tension pneumothorax. What is the most appropriate immediate next step in management?
questions.solution: ent Explanation: In a patient with Tension pneumothorax, the immediate next step in the management would be Airway, breathing, and circulation (ABC) assessment. ATLS protocol/ Advanced Trauma Life Support protocol: This includes both Primary and Secondary assessment. Primary survey: It includes the airway, breathing, circulation, disability or neurologic condition, and exposure and environmental control, which is known by the mnemonic ABCDE. The airway is assessed immediately by a verbal response, and if it is not clear, needful intervention is carried out. Breathing is evaluated by chest movements, breath sounds and saturation, assisted ventilation is provided if needed and needle decompression is done first to relieve pressure in case of Tension pneumothorax (Option A) Circulation assessment includes ruling out shock . IV access and immediate fluid resuscitation are recommended according to the ATLS in case of shock. Neurological assessment is done to assess any traumatic brain or spinal injury and neurogenic shock. The GCS score is evaluated. Environmental control: The patient's clothes should be removed for a thorough examination, and hypothermia should be prevented (warm IV fluids, raised room temperature, body warmers). CT Chest (Option B) is done later, not immediately, as in the primary assessment Chest tube insertion (Option D) is the definitive management, but ABCDE is the part of the primary assessment as per ATLS protocol. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Imipramine and Diphenhydramine are given together to a patient. Why is this combination considered irrational?
questions.stemHtml: Imipramine and Diphenhydramine are given together to a patient. Why is this combination considered irrational?
questions.solution: > Explanation: Imipramine, a tricyclic antidepressant (TCA), and diphenhydramine, a first-generation antihistamine, both exhibit significant anticholinergic properties, hence combining these two drugs is considered irrational because their additive anticholinergic effects. Effects such as drowsiness, blurred vision, dry mouth, heat intolerance, flushing, decreased sweating, difficulty urinating, abdominal cramping, constipation, irregular heartbeat, and confusion. Diphenhydramine does not significantly affect serotonin. Imipramine affects serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake, but the combination does not increase serotonin syndrome risk. (Option B) Imipramine may cause orthostatic hypotension due to alpha-1 blockade, but diphenhydramine generally does not cause significant hypotension. While both can cause sedation , this is not the primary concern . Sedation is common but not necessarily irrational unless it causes functional impairment. Anticholinergic load is the greater clinical concern. @Neet_pg_bot

Medical Management of PPH

Drug

Dose

Key Notes

10-20 units in drip
  • DOC for uterine atony
  • Never give undiluted bolus dose (causes hypotension and arrhythmias)

100 mcg in 1 ml IV over 1 min
  • Synthetic analogue of oxytocin, more sustained release
  • Onset: 2 mins, lasts 1 hour
  • Equivalent to 16 hrs of oxytocin drip

0.2 mg IV (also IM, IV acts faster)

  • Can be given IM but IV acts faster

  • Prostaglandin used for postpartum hemorrhage

  • Contraindications

Carboprost (PGFα)

(Option B ruled out)

250 μg IM, repeat every 15-90 mins (up to 8 doses)
  • Never given IV (causes sudden hypertension)
  • Can be administered intra-myometrial
  • Used when other drugs are ineffective
  • Contraindications: Asthma, pulmonary hypertension, suspected amniotic fluid embolism, and certain renal, liver, and cardiac conditions.

1 g (10 mL of 100 mg/mL solution) intravenously over 10 to 20 minutes

  • Infusion rate should not exceed 1 mL/minute (to avoid hypotension).

questions.stem: Cyanide and carbon monoxide act on which of the heme proteins:
questions.stemHtml: Cyanide and carbon monoxide act on which of the heme proteins:
questions.solution: ong>Explanation: Cyanide (CN⁻) and carbon monoxide (CO) are potent inhibitors of cytochrome c oxidase (Complex IV of the mitochondrial electron transport chain). Cyanide: Binds irreversibly to the heme iron (Fe³⁺) in cytochrome c oxidase, blocking electron transfer to oxygen. Carbon monoxide: Binds competitively to the heme iron (Fe²⁺) in cytochrome c oxidase, displacing oxygen (O₂). Myoglobin (Option B) CO binds to myoglobin (causing cherry-red tissues), but this is not the primary lethal mechanism. Catalase (Option C) Not a target of cyanide/CO toxicity (catalase breaks down H₂O₂, not involved in O₂ utilization). NADH dehydrogenase (Complex I) (Option D) Inhibited by rotenone, not cyanide/CO. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: During recording of EEG, a resting and awake person was instructed to close his eyes and then open them. The dominant wave which decreases on opening the eyes is ?
questions.stemHtml: During recording of EEG, a resting and awake person was instructed to close his eyes and then open them. The dominant wave which decreases on opening the eyes is ?
questions.solution: ong>Explanation: Alpha waves (8–13 Hz) are seen when a person is awake, relaxed, and has their eyes closed. These waves are most prominent in the occipital region of the brain. When the person opens their eyes, alpha wave activity diminishes, a phenomenon known as "alpha block" or "desynchronization." So, alpha waves decrease upon eye opening, even though the person remains awake. Beta waves (13–30 Hz) (Option B) - These are associated with active thinking, attention, and eye opening. Increase, not decrease, when the eyes are opened or during mental activity. Theta waves (4–7 Hz) (Option C) - Seen during light sleep or drowsiness, not in a fully awake person. They are not prominent in a resting, awake person and do not dominate or decrease upon eye opening. Delta waves (0.5–4 Hz) (Option D) - Present during deep sleep (slow-wave sleep),not seen in an awake person. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ong>Explanation:

Alpha waves (8–13 Hz) are seen when a person is awake, relaxed, and has their eyes closed.

These waves are most prominent in the occipital region of the brain. When the person opens their eyes, alpha wave activity diminishes, a phenomenon known as "alpha block" or "desynchronization."

So, alpha waves decrease upon eye opening, even though the person remains awake.

Beta waves (13–30 Hz) (Option B) - These are associated with active thinking, attention, and eye opening. Increase, not decrease, when the eyes are opened or during mental activity.

 

Theta waves (4–7 Hz) (Option C) - Seen during light sleep or drowsiness, not in a fully awake person. They are not prominent in a resting, awake person and do not dominate or decrease upon eye opening.

 

Delta waves (0.5–4 Hz) (Option D) - Present during deep sleep (slow-wave sleep),not seen in an awake person.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old male patient underwent lower abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia. Vecuronium was administered as a muscle relaxant during the procedure. At the end of the surgery, which of the following is the most appropriate agent to reverse the effects of vecuronium?
questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old male patient underwent lower abdominal surgery under general anaesthesia. Vecuronium was administered as a muscle relaxant during the procedure. At the end of the surgery, which of the following is the most appropriate agent to reverse the effects of vecuronium?
questions.solution: uronium is an intermediate-acting Nondepolarizing Muscle Relaxant , and its action is reversed by cholinesterase inhibitors that increase acetylcholine levels . Vecuronium acts by blocking acetylcholine by competitively binding to nicotinic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction, preventing depolarisation. Cholinesterase inhibitors, like neostigmine, increase the levels of acetylcholine at the neuromuscular junction by inhibiting the enzyme that breaks it down, increasing its concentration and restoring muscle activity. Commonly given along with atropine or glycopyrrolate to counteract muscarinic side effects. (Option C) Baclofen (Option B) is a GABA-B receptor agonist used as a muscle relaxant in spasticity. It has no role in reversing neuromuscular blockade, in fact, it causes relaxation , not reversal. Drotaverine (Option D) is an antispasmodic drug used for smooth muscle spasms , like in renal colic or dysmenorrhea. It has no effect on skeletal muscle or neuromuscular blockers. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: n class="customMeta" data-dictid="6edf4961e61692777199edf8feaa6d">surface tension in the alveoli is governed by the fluid lining the alveoli, and it changes with alveolar size. This is primarily regulated by pulmonary surfactant, which reduces surface tension. During inspiration, the alveoli expand and increase in surface area The surfactant becomes more spread out and less concentrated, leading to a relative increase in surface tension. Conversely, during expiration, the alveoli shrink, surfactant becomes more concentrated, and surface tension decreases. This is in accordance with Laplace's Law: P = 2T/r Where: P = pressure required to keep alveolus open T= surface tension r= radius of alveolus As the radius increases (inspiration), surface tension also increases unless adequately countered by surfactant. Change in posture from standing to supine (Option B) - This posture change affects lung volumes and distribution of blood flow, but not directly the surface tension of alveolar fluid. It may affect ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) matching, but not surface tension dynamics directly. Expiration (Option C) - During expiration, alveoli decrease in size. Surfactants become more concentrated, reducing surface tension. Change in posture from supine to standing (Option D) - Similar to option B, this may affect pulmonary perfusion and ventilation, but does not have a direct effect on surface tension of alveolar fluid. @Neet_pg_bot

n class="customMeta" data-dictid="6edf4961e61692777199edf8feaa6d">surface tension in the alveoli is governed by the fluid lining the alveoli, and it changes with alveolar size. This is primarily regulated by pulmonary surfactant, which reduces surface tension.

During inspiration, the alveoli expand and increase in surface area

The surfactant becomes more spread out and less concentrated, leading to a relative increase in surface tension.

Conversely, during expiration, the alveoli shrink, surfactant becomes more concentrated, and surface tension decreases.

This is in accordance with Laplace's Law:

P = 2T/r

Where:

P = pressure required to keep alveolus open

T= surface tension

r= radius of alveolus

As the radius increases (inspiration), surface tension also increases unless adequately countered by surfactant.

 

 

Change in posture from standing to supine (Option B) - This posture change affects lung volumes and distribution of blood flow, but not directly the surface tension of alveolar fluid.

It may affect ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) matching, but not surface tension dynamics directly.

Expiration (Option C) - During expiration, alveoli decrease in size. Surfactants become more concentrated, reducing surface tension.

 

Change in posture from supine to standing (Option D) - Similar to option B, this may affect pulmonary perfusion and ventilation, but does not have a direct effect on surface tension of alveolar fluid.

  • Connective tissue and lymphatics

questions.stem: A newborn baby delivered at 36 weeks of gestation was brought to the OPD with complaints of shortness of breath. The chest x-ray is as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A newborn baby delivered at 36 weeks of gestation was brought to the OPD with complaints of shortness of breath. The chest x-ray is as shown below. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct answer- Option a) Respiratory distress syndrome Low lung volumes: The lungs may appear smaller than normal, and the diaphragm may be elevated, giving a "bell-shaped" thorax. This is because the alveoli have collapsed. Diffuse, bilateral and symmetrical granular opacities (ground-glass appearance): This is the most characteristic finding. It's due to the widespread collapse of the alveoli and atelectasis, making the lung fields appear hazy or finely granular. Air bronchograms: These are visible air-filled bronchi outlined by the surrounding collapsed, opaque lung tissue. They appear as dark, branching structures against the lighter, hazy background. questions.stem: A 26-year-old male presents with complaints of lower abdominal pain, and passage of blood mixed with stools for the past 3 months. Based on his radiological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 26-year-old male presents with complaints of lower abdominal pain, and passage of blood mixed with stools for the past 3 months. Based on his radiological findings, what is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: ion A - Ulcerative Colitis (UC) - Symptoms: Lower abdominal pain: Common in UC, often colicky or cramping. Passage of blood mixed with stools: A cardinal symptom of UC, as the inflammation primarily affects the superficial mucosal lining, leading to friability and bleeding. 3 months duration: Fits the chronic, relapsing-remitting nature of IBD. 26-year-old male: UC commonly presents in young adults. Ulcerative Colitis (UC) - Xrays Loss of haustral markings ("lead pipe" or "garden hose" appearance): This is a classic sign of chronic UC due to continuous inflammation and fibrosis. Incorrect Options: Option B - Pseudomembranous Colitis (PMC) - X-rays: Often non-specific in early or mild cases. Colonic dilatation: Can be diffuse or segmental. Nodular haustral thickening / "Thumbprinting" : This is a relatively classic finding, representing prominent edema and thickening of the haustral folds, and is often more pronounced than in UC. It can also be seen in ischemic colitis. Option C - Crohn's Disease - X-rays: Often normal. Dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels: Suggestive of small bowel obstruction, a common complication due to strictures. "String sign" : Severe narrowing of a segment of bowel, often the terminal ileum, appearing as a thin, continuous string of barium. This indicates a stricture. " Skip lesions ": Inflamed areas separated by normal bowel, a characteristic feature. Difficult to see on plain X-ray, more apparent on barium studies. Option D - Intestinal Tuberculosis (TB) - X-rays: Often non-specific. Ascites: Can be present, especially in peritoneal TB. Absence of gas shadows in the right iliac fossa: Due to thickened, matted bowel loops in the ileocecal region. @Neet_pg_bot

ion A - Ulcerative Colitis (UC) - Symptoms:
  • Lower abdominal pain: Common in UC, often colicky or cramping.
  • Passage of blood mixed with stools: A cardinal symptom of UC, as the inflammation primarily affects the superficial mucosal lining, leading to friability and bleeding.
  • 3 months duration: Fits the chronic, relapsing-remitting nature of IBD.
  • 26-year-old male: UC commonly presents in young adults.

Ulcerative Colitis (UC) - Xrays

  • Loss of haustral markings ("lead pipe" or "garden hose" appearance): This is a classic sign of chronic UC due to continuous inflammation and fibrosis.

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Pseudomembranous Colitis (PMC) - X-rays:

  • Often non-specific in early or mild cases.
  • Colonic dilatation: Can be diffuse or segmental.
  • Nodular haustral thickening / "Thumbprinting": This is a relatively classic finding, representing prominent edema and thickening of the haustral folds, and is often more pronounced than in UC. It can also be seen in ischemic colitis.

Option C - Crohn's Disease - X-rays:

  • Often normal.
  • Dilated loops of small bowel with air-fluid levels: Suggestive of small bowel obstruction, a common complication due to strictures.
  • "String sign": Severe narrowing of a segment of bowel, often the terminal ileum, appearing as a thin, continuous string of barium. This indicates a stricture.
  • "Skip lesions": Inflamed areas separated by normal bowel, a characteristic feature. Difficult to see on plain X-ray, more apparent on barium studies.

Option D - Intestinal Tuberculosis (TB) - X-rays:

  • Often non-specific.
  • Ascites: Can be present, especially in peritoneal TB.
  • Absence of gas shadows in the right iliac fossa: Due to thickened, matted bowel loops in the ileocecal region.

questions.stem: Gastric lavage treated with silver nitrate gives a black colour in poisoning with which of the following?
questions.stemHtml: Gastric lavage treated with silver nitrate gives a black colour in poisoning with which of the following?
questions.solution: um phosphide (ALP) is a pesticide and upon ingestion, it with hydrochloric acid in the stomach to release phosphine gas (PH₃) , which is the primary toxic agent. When silver nitrate (AgNO₃) is added to the gastric lavage or exposed to the gas emitted from the stomach contents , phosphine gas reduces silver nitrate to metallic silver , which appears black . questions.stem: A 30-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast and a fever. On examination, the left breast appears as shown in the image below. There is mild axillary lymphadenopathy on the affected side and the contralateral breast is normal. Repeated aspirations under antibiotic cover were unsuccessful. A USG done showed fluid collection. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old lactating mother presents with pain in her left breast and a fever. On examination, the left breast appears as shown in the image below. There is mild axillary lymphadenopathy on the affected side and the contralateral breast is normal. Repeated aspirations under antibiotic cover were unsuccessful. A USG done showed fluid collection. What is the next best step in the management of this patient?
questions.solution: >Explanation: The clinical scenario described suggests that the patient may have developed a breast abscess. Breast abscesses are typically caused by bacterial infection and are more common in lactating women due to the increased risk of bacterial colonization of the breast ducts. The presence of fever, pain, and fluid collection seen on ultrasound are also consistent with a breast abscess. Repeated aspirations under antibiotic cover have been unsuccessful, suggesting that the abscess is not resolving with conservative management alone. Therefore, the next best step in the management of this patient would be incision and drainage of the abscess. Incision and drainage is the most effective way to treat a breast abscess, as it allows for the complete removal of the infected material and helps to prevent recurrence. Breast Abscess Definition Pus-filled cavity within breast tissue. Types Lactational Abscess: Associated with breastfeeding. Non-Lactational Abscess: Occurs in non-lactating women, e.g., periductal mastitis. Causes and Risk Factors Lactation: Incidence: 3% to 20% in lactating mothers. Common pathogen: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant strains in hospital settings). Entry points: Cracked/retracted nipple, blocked lactiferous ducts. Non-Lactation: Often in nulliparous women or post-lactation. Conditions: Periductal mastitis, idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, tubercular mastitis. Smoking and diabetes as risk factors. Signs and symptoms Fever, leukocytosis, erythema, pain and tenderness, swelling, malaise, difficulty feeding, enlarged and tender axillary nodes Diagnosis Ultrasonography: Detects cellulitis, liquefaction necrosis. Confirms abscess size, location, and loculation. Treatment Lactational Mastitis: Antibiotics: Anti-staphylococcal (e.g., cloxacillin, flucloxacillin, erythromycin). Breast emptying: Frequent breastfeeding or pumping. Support: Breast support garment, cold compresses, analgesia. Drainage: Ultrasound-guided preferred over surgical incision. Follow-up: Regular clinical and ultrasonographic reviews, culture-based antibiotic modification. Non-Lactational Mastitis: Broad-spectrum antibiotics for subareolar infections. Needle aspiration for abscess drainage. Major milk duct excision for complications like sepsis or fistula. Broad-spectrum antibiotics (Option B) may be used in conjunction with incision and drainage to treat the infection, but antibiotics alone are not sufficient for the management of a Breast abscess. Breast conservation surgery (Option C) typically involves the removal of a breast lump or tumor. Thus, breast conservation surgery is not appropriate management option for a breast abscess. Punch biopsy (Option C) is a diagnostic procedure used to obtain a tissue sample for analysis. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
>Explanation:
  • The clinical scenario described suggests that the patient may have developed a breast abscess.
  • Breast abscesses are typically caused by bacterial infection and are more common in lactating women due to the increased risk of bacterial colonization of the breast ducts.
  • The presence of fever, pain, and fluid collection seen on ultrasound are also consistent with a breast abscess.
  • Repeated aspirations under antibiotic cover have been unsuccessful, suggesting that the abscess is not resolving with conservative management alone. Therefore, the next best step in the management of this patient would be incision and drainage of the abscess.
  • Incision and drainage is the most effective way to treat a breast abscess, as it allows for the complete removal of the infected material and helps to prevent recurrence.

Breast Abscess

Definition
  • Pus-filled cavity within breast tissue.

Types
  • Lactational Abscess: Associated with breastfeeding.
  • Non-Lactational Abscess: Occurs in non-lactating women, e.g., periductal mastitis.

Causes and Risk Factors
  • Lactation:
    • Incidence: 3% to 20% in lactating mothers.
    • Common pathogen: Staphylococcus aureus (methicillin-resistant strains in hospital settings).
    • Entry points: Cracked/retracted nipple, blocked lactiferous ducts.
  • Non-Lactation:
    • Often in nulliparous women or post-lactation.
    • Conditions: Periductal mastitis, idiopathic granulomatous mastitis, tubercular mastitis.
    • Smoking and diabetes as risk factors.

Signs and symptoms

Fever, leukocytosis, erythema, pain and tenderness, swelling, malaise, difficulty feeding, enlarged and tender axillary nodes

Diagnosis
  • Ultrasonography:
    • Detects cellulitis, liquefaction necrosis.
    • Confirms abscess size, location, and loculation.

Treatment
  • Lactational Mastitis:
    • Antibiotics: Anti-staphylococcal (e.g., cloxacillin, flucloxacillin, erythromycin).
    • Breast emptying: Frequent breastfeeding or pumping.
    • Support: Breast support garment, cold compresses, analgesia.
    • Drainage: Ultrasound-guided preferred over surgical incision.
    • Follow-up: Regular clinical and ultrasonographic reviews, culture-based antibiotic modification.
  • Non-Lactational Mastitis:
    • Broad-spectrum antibiotics for subareolar infections.
    • Needle aspiration for abscess drainage.
    • Major milk duct excision for complications like sepsis or fistula.

Broad-spectrum antibiotics (Option B) may be used in conjunction with incision and drainage to treat the infection, but antibiotics alone are not sufficient for the management of a Breast abscess.

Breast conservation surgery (Option C) typically involves the removal of a breast lump or tumor. Thus, breast conservation surgery is not appropriate management option for a breast abscess.

Punch biopsy (Option C) is a diagnostic procedure used to obtain a tissue sample for analysis.

questions.stem: IGF-1 and IGF-2 (Insulin-like Growth Factors) are structurally most similar to which of the following molecules?
questions.stemHtml: IGF-1 and IGF-2 (Insulin-like Growth Factors) are structurally most similar to which of the following molecules?
questions.solution: Correct answer: B) Pro-Insulin IGF-1 and IGF-2 (Insulin-like Growth Factors) are named so because their amino acid sequence and tertiary structure closely resemble insulin . They are single-chain polypeptides with structural similarity to proinsulin rather than mature insulin, since they retain a connecting region analogous to the C-peptide in proinsulin. (Option B) Insulin (Option A): Mature insulin has two separate chains (A and B) linked by disulfide bonds, whereas IGFs remain as a single chain. C-peptide (Option C) alone is just the connecting peptide, not structurally resembling IGFs. Preproinsulin (Option D) has a signal peptide for secretion, which is not a feature of IGFs. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct answer: B) Pro-Insulin

 

IGF-1 and IGF-2 (Insulin-like Growth Factors) are named so because their amino acid sequence and tertiary structure closely resemble insulin.

They are single-chain polypeptides with structural similarity to proinsulin rather than mature insulin, since they retain a connecting region analogous to the C-peptide in proinsulin. (Option B)
 

Insulin (Option A): Mature insulin has two separate chains (A and B) linked by disulfide bonds, whereas IGFs remain as a single chain.
 

C-peptide (Option C) alone is just the connecting peptide, not structurally resembling IGFs.
 

Preproinsulin (Option D) has a signal peptide for secretion, which is not a feature of IGFs.

questions.stem: Which investigation is most useful for visualizing the individual layers of the retina?

questions.solution: Coherence Tomography (OCT) (Option B): Most useful. Provides high-resolution, cross-sectional images. questions.stemHtml: A 62-year-old male presents with sudden onset of shortness of breath and B/L pedal edema. He is compliant with his antihypertensive medications, and blood pressure is well controlled. ECG reveals an ejection fraction of 60%, concentric left ventricular hypertrophy, left atrial enlargement, and grade 2 diastolic dysfunction. Which of the following is the most appropriate next step to improve his condition?

options.label: B
