questions.answerText: Initiate loop diuretics and SGLT2 inhibitors for management of HFpEF
questions.solution: shortness of breath and bilateral pedal edema, classic signs of heart failure. His echocardiogram findings show: Ejection fraction (EF) of 60% → Preserved systolic function Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy Left atrial enlargement Grade 2 diastolic dysfunction These findings support a diagnosis of Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF), which is often related to diastolic dysfunction, especially in older adults with hypertension-induced hypertrophy. Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) help relieve volume overload symptoms like dyspnea and edema. SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) have been shown in recent trials to reduce hospitalization and improve quality of life in HFpEF , regardless of diabetes status . This is the most appropriate and guideline-recommended management . Types of heart failure: HFrEF: Systolic dysfunction, may present acutely. HFpEF: Diastolic dysfunction, usually present as chronic heart failure. Management of CHF: First line drugs used in chronic Heart failure: (mortality-reducing drugs) ARBs/ACE-Inhibitors Beta blockers (2nd gen- cardioselective) SGLT-2 inhibitors (Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin) Anti-aldosterone (Spironolactone) Acute cases with Pulmonary edema: Oxygen: Secure airway and supplement O2 Loop diuretics: IV Furosemide 20-80 mg , reduces preload and systemic venous congestion IV Morphine: if patient is in severe pain/distress, can cause respiratory depression IV Nitroglycerin infusion: reduce afterload Acute decompensated with cardiogenic shock: (low BP) Vasopressors: Norepinephrine, Dobutamine, Dopamine Inodilators: Milrinone & Amrinone Levosimendan: Ca2+ channel sensitizer Omecamtiv mecarbil: Direct myosin activator Non-pharmacological treatment: Implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICD) Coronary revascularisation: in Coronary artery disease patients Ventricular assist devices Cardiac transplantation Incorrect Options: Perform coronary angiography to rule out ischemic cardiomyopathy (Option A): Coronary angiography is appropriate if ischemic heart disease is strongly suspected. However, this patient has preserved EF and concentric LVH , which more strongly points toward hypertensive heart disease and HFpEF , not ischemic cardiomyopathy. This is not the most appropriate first step . Start digoxin to enhance myocardial contractility (Option C): Digoxin is not indicated in HFpEF, especially when EF is preserved and there is no indication of systolic dysfunction or atrial fibrillation needing rate control. It is not helpful here. Initiate ivabradine to reduce heart rate and improve diastolic filling (Option D): Ivabradine is indicated in HFrEF with EF ≤35% and sinus rhythm with heart rate ≥70 bpm , despite beta-blockers. It does not have a proven role in HFpEF . @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
shortness of breath and bilateral pedal edema, classic signs of heart failure. His echocardiogram findings show:
  • Ejection fraction (EF) of 60% → Preserved systolic function
  • Concentric left ventricular hypertrophy
  • Left atrial enlargement
  • Grade 2 diastolic dysfunction

These findings support a diagnosis of Heart Failure with Preserved Ejection Fraction (HFpEF), which is often related to diastolic dysfunction, especially in older adults with hypertension-induced hypertrophy.

  • Loop diuretics (e.g., furosemide) help relieve volume overload symptoms like dyspnea and edema.
  • SGLT2 inhibitors (e.g., empagliflozin, dapagliflozin) have been shown in recent trials to reduce hospitalization and improve quality of life in HFpEF, regardless of diabetes status.
  • This is the most appropriate and guideline-recommended management.

Types of heart failure:

  • HFrEF: Systolic dysfunction, may present acutely.
  • HFpEF: Diastolic dysfunction, usually present as chronic heart failure.

Management of CHF:

First line drugs used in chronic Heart failure: (mortality-reducing drugs)
  • ARBs/ACE-Inhibitors
  • Beta blockers (2nd gen- cardioselective)
  • SGLT-2 inhibitors (Dapagliflozin, Empagliflozin)
  • Anti-aldosterone (Spironolactone)

Acute cases with Pulmonary edema:
  • Oxygen: Secure airway and supplement O2
  • Loop diuretics: IV Furosemide 20-80 mg, reduces preload and systemic venous congestion
  • IV Morphine: if patient is in severe pain/distress, can cause respiratory depression
  • IV Nitroglycerin infusion: reduce afterload

Acute decompensated with cardiogenic shock: (low BP)
  • Vasopressors: Norepinephrine, Dobutamine, Dopamine
  • Inodilators: Milrinone & Amrinone
  • Levosimendan: Ca2+ channel sensitizer
  • Omecamtiv mecarbil: Direct myosin activator

Non-pharmacological treatment:
  • Implantable cardioverter defibrillators (ICD)
  • Coronary revascularisation: in Coronary artery disease patients
  • Ventricular assist devices
  • Cardiac transplantation

Incorrect Options:

Perform coronary angiography to rule out ischemic cardiomyopathy (Option A): Coronary angiography is appropriate if ischemic heart disease is strongly suspected. However, this patient has preserved EF and concentric LVH, which more strongly points toward hypertensive heart disease and HFpEF, not ischemic cardiomyopathy. This is not the most appropriate first step.

Start digoxin to enhance myocardial contractility (Option C): Digoxin is not indicated in HFpEF, especially when EF is preserved and there is no indication of systolic dysfunction or atrial fibrillation needing rate control. It is not helpful here.

Initiate ivabradine to reduce heart rate and improve diastolic filling (Option D): Ivabradine is indicated in HFrEF with EF ≤35% and sinus rhythm with heart rate ≥70 bpm, despite beta-blockers. It does not have a proven role in HFpEF.

questions.stem: Which of the following brain regions is primarily associated with the processing of explicit memory?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following brain regions is primarily associated with the processing of explicit memory?
questions.solution: Correct Answer- a) Hippocampus The brain region primarily associated with the processing of explicit memory is the hippocampus . Explicit memory, also known as declarative memory, involves the conscious recollection of facts and events. This includes episodic memory (personal experiences) and semantic memory (general knowledge). Amygdala (Option B): Primarily involved in processing emotions and attaching emotional significance to memories, particularly fear. While it influences memory, it's not the primary site for forming or retrieving explicit factual memories. Insular cortex(Option C): Involved in a wide range of functions including interoception (awareness of internal bodily states), emotion, taste, and some aspects of recognition memory, but not the primary hub for explicit memory formation. Prefrontal cortex(Option D): Crucial for working memory , executive functions, decision-making, and the retrieval and organization of long-term memories, but the hippocampus is the key structure for the initial formation and indexing of new explicit memories. Long-term storage of explicit memories is thought to ultimately reside in the neocortex, with the hippocampus playing a critical role in their consolidation and retrieval. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: a progressive, asymptomatic lesion over the neck, clinically suggestive of Lupus Vulgaris (a form of cutaneous tuberculosis), the most helpful investigation would be skin biopsy and TB workup. It is a chronic, progressive, paucibacillary (not multibacillary) form of cutaneous tuberculosis. Lupus vulgaris is the most common form of cutaneous TB seen in adults (M/C in females). Causative organisms: Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycobacterium bovis. Pathogenesis : Route of spread: Endogenous spread or from exogenous inoculation. It occurs in a previously sensitized individual with an increased cell-mediated immunity to tuberculin. Clinical features: Presents as a single or a group of erythematous violaceous annular plaques with central scarring and atrophy with active margins. The periphery shows erythematous deep-seated nodules which on diascopy may stand out as apple jelly nodules. Most commonly seen in the buttocks, upper extremities, and face. Papules may recur within scarred areas, enlarging and coalescing into large, firm, elevated plaques. Treatment: Antitibercular therapy. Complication: Secondary scarring and squamous cell carcinoma may develop rarely. KOH preparation (Option 1) is used to detect superficial fungal infections like tinea or candidiasis by identifying fungal elements in skin scrapings. Since lupus vulgaris is a form of cutaneous tuberculosis, KOH is not helpful for its diagnosis. HIV testing (Option 4) is useful in immunocompromised patients or atypical infections, but this patient has a localized, slow-growing lesion without systemic signs. It doesn't directly help diagnose lupus vulgaris and isn't a first-line test. @Neet_pg_bot

-dictid="68f01c7242169277718571a7e5e75c">defecography (or defecating proctography) is a dynamic fluoroscopic study using barium paste to visualize anorectal function during simulated defecation.

Key X-ray Findings:

  • Anorectal Angle (ARA): Measured between the rectum and anal canal. Normally widens (becomes more obtuse) during defecation. Anismus shows paradoxical narrowing.
  • Perineal Descent: Downward movement of the pelvic floor. Excessive descent indicates laxity/weakness.
  • Rectal Emptying: Assesses completeness of barium expulsion. Incomplete emptying suggests obstruction.
  • Prolapse:
    • Rectocele: Anterior rectal bulging into the vagina.
    • Intussusception: Rectal wall telescoping into the lumen.
    • Rectal Prolapse: Rectum extending into or outside the anal canal.
    • Enterocele: Small bowel herniating into the rectovaginal space.
  • Anal Canal: Assesses opening during evacuation and closure during contraction.

questions.solutionHtml:
ypes – IgA1 and IgA2
  • Major immunoglobulin in colostrum, saliva, and tears
  • Two Forms: Monomeric serum IgA and dimeric secretory IgA
  • Secretory IgA:
    • Two monomer units joined together at their carboxy terminals by a glycopeptide termed the J chain
    • Produced by plasma cells near mucosal or glandular epithelium
    • Secretory piece or secretory component in the IgA protects IgA from bacterial proteases, especially in areas with abundant bacterial flora (e.g., intestines)
    • Role in Local Immunity: Concentrated in secretions, it forms an "antibody paste" on mucosal surfaces to protect against respiratory and intestinal pathogens.
    • Resistance: Relatively resistant to digestive enzymes and reducing agents
    • Activates the alternative complement pathway.

    • Immunoglobulin

    Properties

    Structure

    IgA

    Found in mucous, saliva, tears and breast milk.

    Protects against pathogens.

    IgD

    Part of the B cell receptor

    Activates basophils and mast cells.

    IgE

    Protects against parasitic worms.

    Responsible for allergic reactions.

    IgG

    Secreted by plasma cells in the blood.

    Able to cross the placenta into the fetus.

    IgM

    May be attached to the surface of a B cell or secreted into blood.

    Responsible for early stages of immunity.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not an effective treatment for amblyopia?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is not an effective treatment for amblyopia?

options.label: D
options.text: Use of video games for visual stimulation

questions.solution: 4f9bb384">Strabismus surgery Explanation Correction of refractive errors (Option A ruled out) : This is a fundamental and often the first step in amblyopia treatment. Uncorrected significant refractive errors (like high farsightedness, nearsightedness, or astigmatism) can prevent clear image formation and lead to amblyopia. Correcting these errors with glasses or contact lenses allows the brain to receive a clear image, which is essential for visual development. This is an effective treatment. Occlusion therapy (patching) (Option B rule out) : This is a cornerstone of amblyopia treatment. It involves covering the stronger, non-amblyopic eye for specific periods each day, forcing the brain to use and develop the weaker, amblyopic eye. This is a highly effective and widely used treatment. Strabismus surgery (Option C) : Strabismus (misalignment of the eyes) is a common cause of amblyopia. While strabismus surgery can align the eyes, it primarily addresses the cosmetic and functional alignment issue. It does not directly treat the amblyopia itself, which is a brain-based vision deficit. However, aligning the eyes before or during amblyopia treatment can sometimes improve the chances of success, especially in preventing suppression. It is not a direct or primary treatment for the amblyopia deficit itself, but for its cause. Use of video games for visual stimulation (Option D rule out) : There has been research into using specially designed video games (often dichoptic, where each eye sees different parts of the game) to stimulate both eyes simultaneously and improve visual acuity in amblyopia. While this is a newer and emerging area of research, it has shown promise as an adjunctive or alternative therapy, particularly in older children or those who don't tolerate patching well. This is considered an emerging and potentially effective treatment. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A biopsy of a patient presenting with painful vesicular lesions and superficial erosions in the genital area is shown. What treatment would you initiate?
questions.stemHtml: A biopsy of a patient presenting with painful vesicular lesions and superficial erosions in the genital area is shown. What treatment would you initiate?
questions.solution: xplanation: The biopsy image, along with the presence of painful vesicular lesions and superficial erosions in the genital area, is indicative of Genital Herpes , most commonly caused by the Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV). The appropriate treatment for this condition is acyclovir. Treatment : First line Acyclovir (topical/oral) (Option A) Hydrocolloid dressing Topical penciclovir Second line Long-term prophylactic acyclovir Third line IV acyclovir Penciclovir Foscarnet IV cidofovir Topical imiquimod Incorrect Options: Steroids (Option B) are not suitable for treating genital herpes because they suppress the immune response. While steroids can be useful in managing inflammatory or autoimmune conditions, using them during an active viral infection like herpes simplex virus (HSV) can worsen the condition. Penicillin (Option C) is an antibiotic used primarily to treat bacterial infections, such as syphilis. Syphilis typically presents with a painless ulcer (chancre), in contrast to the painful vesicular lesions and superficial erosions seen in genital herpes. Azithromycin (Option D) is another antibiotic, commonly used to treat bacterial sexually transmitted infections (STIs) such as chlamydia and, in some cases, gonorrhea. However, like penicillin, azithromycin has no antiviral activity and is ineffective against HSV. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is not a mechanism of action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH)?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is not a mechanism of action of antidiuretic hormone (ADH)?

options.label: A
options.text: a. Increase absorption of urea in medullary duct

options.label: B
options.text: Increase absorption of urea in descending loop of Henle

options.label: C
options.text: Decrease absorption of NaCl in ascending loop of Henle

options.label: D
options.text: Increase water permeability in the collecting ducts

questions.answerText: a. Increase absorption of urea in medullary duct
questions.solution: Correct answer- a. Increase absorption of urea in medullary duct: TRUE. ADH increases the permeability of the inner medullary collecting duct to urea, primarily by upregulating urea transporters (UT-A1 and UT-A3). This is crucial for maintaining the medullary osmotic gradient, which is essential for water reabsorption. b. Increase absorption of urea in descending loop of Henle: FALSE. The descending limb of the loop of Henle is highly permeable to water but relatively impermeable to urea . Urea is actually secreted into the thin ascending limb of the loop of Henle as part of the urea recycling process, not absorbed in the descending limb under ADH influence. c. Decrease absorption of NaCl in ascending loop of Henle: FALSE. ADH actually increases NaCl reabsorption in the thick ascending limb of the loop of Henle. It does this by increasing the expression and activity of the Na-K-2Cl cotransporter (NKCC2). This action contributes to the countercurrent multiplication mechanism, further concentrating the medullary interstitium and facilitating water reabsorption in the collecting ducts. d. Increase water permeability in the collecting ducts: TRUE. This is a primary and most well-known action of ADH. ADH binds to V2 receptors on the principal cells of the collecting ducts (and late distal tubule), leading to the insertion of aquaporin-2 (AQP2) water channels into the apical membrane. This greatly increases the water permeability of these segments, allowing water to be reabsorbed from the filtrate back into the hypertonic medullary interstitium, thus concentrating the urine. Based on this analysis, the statement that is not a mechanism of action of ADH is: b. Increase absorption of urea in descending loop of Henle c. Decrease absorption of NaCl in ascending loop of Henle Both b and c describe actions that are opposite to or not characteristic of ADH's known effects. However, usually, questions like this have only one definitively incorrect option. Let's re-evaluate more strictly: ADH does increase urea reabsorption, but specifically in the medullary collecting duct , not the descending loop of Henle. So (b) is definitively incorrect regarding location. ADH increases NaCl reabsorption in the thick ascending limb, so (c) stating "decrease absorption" is definitively incorrect. Between (b) and (c), both are incorrect statements about ADH's mechanism. However, (c) describes an action that is the opposite of what ADH does to NaCl reabsorption in that segment, while (b) describes a location where ADH doesn't primarily act on urea reabsorption. In multiple-choice questions seeking the "not a mechanism," the statement that is factually opposite is often the intended answer. Therefore, the most definitively incorrect statement as a mechanism of action of ADH is c. Decrease absorption of NaCl in the ascending loop of Henle. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: CT scans (Option A) use X-rays, which are a form of ionizing radiation. questions.stem: A patient underwent a bone marrow transplant without HLA matching. In which of the following disorders transplant rejection does not occur:
questions.stemHtml: A patient underwent a bone marrow transplant without HLA matching. In which of the following disorders transplant rejection does not occur:
questions.solution: Bone marrow transplant (BMT) rejection is mediated by recipient T lymphocytes recognizing donor HLA antigens as foreign. Therefore, the integrity and function of recipient T cells (especially CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells) are crucial for mounting a rejection response. Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome (BLS): It is a type of MHC class II deficiency , and in some forms, MHC class I expression is also defective. Because of absent or defective HLA expression , CD4⁺ (helper) and sometimes CD8⁺ (cytotoxic) T cells are profoundly dysfunctional or absent. Result: These patients are immunologically unable to recognize or reject transplanted tissue , even in the absence of HLA matching. Hence, rejection does not occur in BLS due to lack of HLA molecule expression and impaired T cell function . Chediak-Higashi Syndrome (Option B) is an autosomal recessive condition with defect in lysosomal trafficking regulator gene (LYST), leading to defective neutrophil function. T and B cell immunity is relatively intact — rejection is possible. Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (Option C) X-linked disorder with combined immunodeficiency, characterized by thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infection. It is caused by mutations in the gene located at Xp11.23 that encodes Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP). Although T-cell dysfunction is present, it is not severe enough to completely prevent rejection . Job’s Syndrome (Hyper-IgE syndrome) (Option C) Impaired Th17 pathway with eosinophilia and recurrent infections. T cell immunity is abnormal but not absent , so rejection can occur . Syndrome T Cell Function Graft Rejection Expected? Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome Severely impaired/absent ❌ No rejection Chediak-Higashi Syndrome Mostly intact ✅ Yes Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome Impaired, not absent ✅ Possible Job's Syndrome Impaired Th17 cells ✅ Possible @Neet_pg_bot

• Bone marrow transplant (BMT) rejection is mediated by recipient T lymphocytes recognizing donor HLA antigens as foreign. Therefore, the integrity and function of recipient T cells (especially CD8⁺ cytotoxic T cells) are crucial for mounting a rejection response.

Bare Lymphocyte Syndrome (BLS):

  • It is a type of MHC class II deficiency, and in some forms, MHC class I expression is also defective.
  • Because of absent or defective HLA expression, CD4⁺ (helper) and sometimes CD8⁺ (cytotoxic) T cells are profoundly dysfunctional or absent.
  • Result: These patients are immunologically unable to recognize or reject transplanted tissue, even in the absence of HLA matching.

Hence, rejection does not occur in BLS due to lack of HLA molecule expression and impaired T cell function.

Chediak-Higashi Syndrome (Option B) is an autosomal recessive condition with defect in lysosomal trafficking regulator gene (LYST), leading to defective neutrophil function.

T and B cell immunity is relatively intact — rejection is possible.

Wiskott-Aldrich Syndrome (Option C) X-linked disorder with combined immunodeficiency, characterized by thrombocytopenia, eczema, and recurrent infection. It is caused by mutations in the gene located at Xp11.23 that encodes Wiskott-Aldrich syndrome protein (WASP). Although T-cell dysfunction is present, it is not severe enough to completely prevent rejection.

Job’s Syndrome (Hyper-IgE syndrome) (Option C) Impaired Th17 pathway with eosinophilia and recurrent infections. T cell immunity is abnormal but not absent, so rejection can occur.

questions.stem: Which of the following statements about Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is incorrect?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements about Multiple Sclerosis (MS) is incorrect?

options.label: A
options.text: 70% of patients with MS develop optic neuritis during course of illness

options.label: B
options.text: Oral steroids are given for acute relapses

options.label: C
options.text: Loss of color perception and depth perception is proportional to visual loss

options.label: D
options.text: Examination of fundus can be normal and can show papillitis

questions.answerText: Loss of color perception and depth perception is proportional to visual loss
questions.solution: > compared to overall visual acuity. A patient may have mild visual acuity loss but significant dyschromatopsia (color desaturation) or depth perception difficulties . Multiple sclerosis (MS) Clinical features: Abrupt or insidious onset of symptoms Sensory symptoms Paresthesias: tingling, prickling sensations, “pins and needles,” or painful burning. Hypesthesia: reduced sensation, numbness, or a “dead” feeling. Unpleasant sensations: feelings that body parts are swollen, wet, raw, or tightly wrapped. Pain is a common symptom of MS. Optic neuritis (ON) Diminished visual acuity. Decreased colour perception in the central field of vision. May progress to severe visual loss. Periorbital pain. Fundoscopic examination: normal or optic disc swelling (papillitis), pallor of the optic disc (optic atrophy). Weakness of the limbs Loss of strength, speed, dexterity, and gait disturbance. Exercise-induced weakness is a characteristic symptom of MS. Upper motor neuron type weakness accompanied by other pyramidal signs. Facial weakness Lesion in the pons may resemble idiopathic Bell’s palsy. Spasticity Spontaneous and movement-induced muscle spasms. Painful spasms. Visual blurring Due to ON (optic neuritis) or diplopia. Diplopia is caused by internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) or palsy of the sixth cranial nerve. Bilateral INO is particularly suggestive of MS. Other gaze disturbances in MS: Horizontal gaze palsy One-and-a-half syndrome (horizontal gaze palsy plus an INO) Acquired pendular nystagmus Ataxia Cerebellar tremors. Cerebellar dysarthria. Vertigo Lesion in the brainstem. Ancillary symptoms Paroxysmal symptoms Brief duration (10s to 2 min), high frequency (5–40 episodes per day), no change of consciousness or change in background electroencephalogram during episodes, and a self-limited course. Lhermitte’s symptom An electric shock-like sensation that radiates down the back into the legs. Typically induced by flexion or other movements of the neck. Trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, and glossopharyngeal neuralgia Demyelinating lesions involve the root entry or exit zone of the fifth, seventh, and ninth cranial nerve, respectively. Facial myokymia Persistent rapid flickering contractions of the facial musculature Slow spread of contraction across the face. Heat sensitivity Uthoff symptoms: Neurological symptoms develop from heat exposure, such as steam baths and saunas. Bladder dysfunction Present in >90% of MS patients. Detrusor hyperreflexia. Detrusor sphincter dyssynergia - hesitancy, urinary retention, overflow incontinence, and recurrent infection. Bowel dysfunction Constipation, faecal urgency or bowel incontinence. Cognitive dysfunction Memory loss. Impaired attention. Psychiatric symptom Depression. Fatigue 90% of patients experience fatigue. It causes work-related disability. Incorrect Options: 70% of patients with MS develop optic neuritis during course of illness (Option A): Optic neuritis is a common presenting symptom and complication of MS. Around 70% of patients develop it at some point during the disease. It often causes painful vision loss, especially on eye movement. Oral steroids are given for acute relapses (Option B): High-dose intravenous steroids (e.g., methylprednisolone) are preferred for acute relapses, but oral steroids (like oral prednisolone or tapering doses after IV) can also be used in certain cases. So, oral steroids are indeed part of acute relapse management, especially during recovery or tapering phases. Examination of fundus can be normal and can show papillitis (Option D): In optic neuritis, retrobulbar neuritis often shows a normal fundus because the inflammation is behind the globe. However, in some cases, papillitis (optic disc swelling) may be seen. Both scenarios are possible in MS-related optic neuritis. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
> compared to overall visual acuity. A patient may have mild visual acuity loss but significant dyschromatopsia (color desaturation) or depth perception difficulties.

Multiple sclerosis (MS) Clinical features:

  • Abrupt or insidious onset of symptoms

Sensory symptoms
  • Paresthesias: tingling, prickling sensations, “pins and needles,” or painful burning.
  • Hypesthesia: reduced sensation, numbness, or a “dead” feeling.
  • Unpleasant sensations: feelings that body parts are swollen, wet, raw, or tightly wrapped.
  • Pain is a common symptom of MS.

Optic neuritis (ON)

  • Diminished visual acuity.
  • Decreased colour perception in the central field of vision.
  • May progress to severe visual loss.
  • Periorbital pain.
  • Fundoscopic examination: normal or optic disc swelling (papillitis), pallor of the optic disc (optic atrophy).

Weakness of the limbs
  • Loss of strength, speed, dexterity, and gait disturbance.
  • Exercise-induced weakness is a characteristic symptom of MS.
  • Upper motor neuron type weakness accompanied by other pyramidal signs.

Facial weakness
  • Lesion in the pons may resemble idiopathic Bell’s palsy.

Spasticity
  • Spontaneous and movement-induced muscle spasms.
  • Painful spasms.

Visual blurring
  • Due to ON (optic neuritis) or diplopia.
  • Diplopia is caused by internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) or palsy of the sixth cranial nerve.
  • Bilateral INO is particularly suggestive of MS.
  • Other gaze disturbances in MS:
    • Horizontal gaze palsy
    • One-and-a-half syndrome (horizontal gaze palsy plus an INO)
    • Acquired pendular nystagmus

Ataxia
  • Cerebellar tremors.
  • Cerebellar dysarthria.

Vertigo
  • Lesion in the brainstem.

 

Ancillary symptoms

Paroxysmal symptoms

Brief duration (10s to 2 min), high frequency (5–40 episodes per day), no change of consciousness or change in background electroencephalogram during episodes, and a self-limited course.

Lhermitte’s symptom

An electric shock-like sensation that radiates down the back into the legs.

Typically induced by flexion or other movements of the neck.

Trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, and glossopharyngeal neuralgia

Demyelinating lesions involve the root entry or exit zone of the fifth, seventh, and ninth cranial nerve, respectively.

Facial myokymia

Persistent rapid flickering contractions of the facial musculature

Slow spread of contraction across the face.

Heat sensitivity

Uthoff symptoms: Neurological symptoms develop from heat exposure, such as steam baths and saunas.

Bladder dysfunction

Present in >90% of MS patients.

Detrusor hyperreflexia.

Detrusor sphincter dyssynergia - hesitancy, urinary retention, overflow incontinence, and recurrent infection.

Bowel dysfunction

Constipation, faecal urgency or bowel incontinence.

Cognitive dysfunction

Memory loss.

Impaired attention.

Psychiatric symptom

Depression.

Fatigue

90% of patients experience fatigue.

It causes work-related disability.

Incorrect Options:

70% of patients with MS develop optic neuritis during course of illness (Option A): Optic neuritis is a common presenting symptom and complication of MS. Around 70% of patients develop it at some point during the disease. It often causes painful vision loss, especially on eye movement.

Oral steroids are given for acute relapses (Option B): High-dose intravenous steroids (e.g., methylprednisolone) are preferred for acute relapses, but oral steroids (like oral prednisolone or tapering doses after IV) can also be used in certain cases. So, oral steroids are indeed part of acute relapse management, especially during recovery or tapering phases.

Examination of fundus can be normal and can show papillitis (Option D): In optic neuritis, retrobulbar neuritis often shows a normal fundus because the inflammation is behind the globe. However, in some cases, papillitis (optic disc swelling) may be seen. Both scenarios are possible in MS-related optic neuritis.

questions.stem: A 3-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a history of cyanosis since infancy. Which of the following is a component of Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)?
questions.stemHtml: A 3-year-old child is brought to the clinic with a history of cyanosis since infancy. Which of the following is a component of Tetralogy of Fallot (TOF)?
questions.solution: db90c23">pulmonary stenosis Explanation: Tetralogy of Fallot is a congenital heart defect characterized by four distinct anomalies: Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD): A hole between the right and left ventricles. Pulmonary Stenosis: Narrowing of the pulmonary outflow tract. This can be subvalvular (infundibular, below the valve), valvular (at the valve), or supravalvular (above the valve). Infundibular pulmonary stenosis is a common and characteristic component. Overriding Aorta: The aorta (the main artery carrying oxygenated blood to the body) is positioned directly over the VSD, receiving blood from both ventricles. Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH): The right ventricle thickens due to the increased workload of pumping blood against the narrowed pulmonary artery and into the aorta. The options provided Inter atrial septal defect (ASD) (Option A ruled out) : While an ASD can coexist with TOF (forming Pentalogy of Fallot), it is not a primary component of the classic Tetralogy of Fallot. Infundibular pulmonary stenosis (Option B) : This is a core component of Tetralogy of Fallot. The narrowing in the outflow tract of the right ventricle is often in the infundibular region. Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH) (Option C ruled out) : In TOF, it's the right ventricle that undergoes hypertrophy due to the increased pressure load. Left ventricular hypertrophy is not a typical feature. Transposition of the great arteries (TGA) (Option D ruled out) : TGA is a completely separate and distinct complex congenital heart defect where the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. It is not a component of TOF. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
db90c23">pulmonary stenosis

Explanation:

Tetralogy of Fallot is a congenital heart defect characterized by four distinct anomalies:

  1. Ventricular Septal Defect (VSD): A hole between the right and left ventricles.
  2. Pulmonary Stenosis: Narrowing of the pulmonary outflow tract. This can be subvalvular (infundibular, below the valve), valvular (at the valve), or supravalvular (above the valve). Infundibular pulmonary stenosis is a common and characteristic component.
  3. Overriding Aorta: The aorta (the main artery carrying oxygenated blood to the body) is positioned directly over the VSD, receiving blood from both ventricles.
  4. Right Ventricular Hypertrophy (RVH): The right ventricle thickens due to the increased workload of pumping blood against the narrowed pulmonary artery and into the aorta.

The options provided

  • Inter atrial septal defect (ASD) (Option A ruled out): While an ASD can coexist with TOF (forming Pentalogy of Fallot), it is not a primary component of the classic Tetralogy of Fallot.
  • Infundibular pulmonary stenosis(Option B): This is a core component of Tetralogy of Fallot. The narrowing in the outflow tract of the right ventricle is often in the infundibular region.
  • Left ventricular hypertrophy (LVH)(Option C ruled out): In TOF, it's the right ventricle that undergoes hypertrophy due to the increased pressure load. Left ventricular hypertrophy is not a typical feature.
  • Transposition of the great arteries (TGA)(Option D ruled out): TGA is a completely separate and distinct complex congenital heart defect where the aorta arises from the right ventricle and the pulmonary artery from the left ventricle. It is not a component of TOF.

questions.stem: A woman with a strong family history of breast and ovarian cancer is being evaluated for BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to detect multiple mutations at different codons in these genes?
questions.stemHtml: A woman with a strong family history of breast and ovarian cancer is being evaluated for BRCA1/BRCA2 mutations. Which of the following is the most appropriate test to detect multiple mutations at different codons in these genes?
questions.solution: The most appropriate test to detect multiple mutations at different codons in BRCA1/BRCA2 genes is Next-generation sequencing (NGS) or Digital Droplet PCR. It is a revolutionary method for rapid, high-throughput DNA and RNA sequencing. Enables massive parallel sequencing of hundreds to thousands of genes or whole genomes. Significantly faster and more comprehensive than traditional methods like Sanger sequencing. Integrates: Advanced sequencing chemistries Diverse sequencing platforms Robust bioinformatics tools Widely used for: Disease diagnosis and prognosis Therapy selection Patient monitoring qPCR (Option A) measures gene expression levels, not specific DNA mutations. RT-PCR (Option B) detects RNA-level changes, limited for comprehensive mutation scanning. Northern blot (Option C) analyzes RNA expression, not DNA mutations. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
The most appropriate test to detect multiple mutations at different codons in BRCA1/BRCA2 genes is Next-generation sequencing (NGS) or Digital Droplet PCR.

  • It is a revolutionary method for rapid, high-throughput DNA and RNA sequencing.
  • Enables massive parallel sequencing of hundreds to thousands of genes or whole genomes.
  • Significantly faster and more comprehensive than traditional methods like Sanger sequencing.
  • Integrates:
    • Advanced sequencing chemistries
    • Diverse sequencing platforms
    • Robust bioinformatics tools
  • Widely used for:
    • Disease diagnosis and prognosis
    • Therapy selection
    • Patient monitoring

 

qPCR (Option A) measures gene expression levels, not specific DNA mutations.
 

RT-PCR (Option B) detects RNA-level changes, limited for comprehensive mutation scanning.
 

Northern blot (Option C) analyzes RNA expression, not DNA mutations.

questions.stem: Which of the following cancers is NOT related to obesity?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following cancers is NOT related to obesity?
questions.solution: /p> Meningiomas are typically benign central nervous system tumors arising from the meninges. Although some observational studies have noted a possible link between obesity and meningioma (particularly in women), this association is not considered well established or causal. Obesity is a well-established risk factor for numerous malignancies , particularly those influenced by chronic inflammation , insulin resistance , and hormonal imbalances . The cancers most strongly linked to obesity include: Endometrial Breast (postmenopausal) Colorectal Esophageal (adenocarcinoma) Pancreatic (Option C) Renal cell carcinoma Gallbladder Liver Gastric (cardia type) (Option B) Multiple myeloma (Option D) These associations are supported by robust epidemiological data and acknowledged by major health organizations (e.g., IARC, WHO, CDC). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: yphae Explanation: An immunocompromised patient, such as one with HIV/AIDS , presenting with dysphagia, odynophagia, and white plaques on esophageal endoscopy, is showing classic signs of esophageal candidiasis, most commonly caused by Candida albicans; microscopic examination (via biopsy or KOH prep) typically reveals diagnostic yeast cells with pseudohyphae. CDC-AIDS defining conditions: Candidiasis of the bronchi, trachea, oesophagal or lungs. (Option A) Cryptosporidiosis with diarrhoea (for longer than 1 month) Cytomegalovirus disease (other than liver, spleen, or nodes), beginning when older than one month Herpes simplex: chronic ulcers (lasting longer than 1 month); or bronchitis, pneumonitis, or esophagitis (beginning when older than one month) Kaposi sarcoma Lymphoma, primary, of brain Mycobacterium avium complex (type of bacterial infection) or M. kansasii, disseminated or extrapulmonary Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP) Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy Toxoplasmosis of the brain, beginning when older than one month Acid-fast bacilli (Option B) are typically associated with infections caused by Mycobacterium species, such as tuberculosis or Mycobacterium avium complex. Their clinical presentation and diagnostic approach differ significantly; diagnosis relies on acid-fast staining of tissue or bodily fluids, rather than endoscopic findings of white esophageal plaques, which are more characteristic of fungal infections like candidiasis. Branching septate hyphae at a 45-degree angle (Option C) is a hallmark of Aspergillus species, a type of mold that most commonly infects the lungs or sinuses, especially in immunocompromised individuals. Additionally, when Aspergillus does infect mucosal tissues, it does not produce the white plaque-like lesions seen in esophageal candidiasis. Multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear inclusions (Option D) are classic histological findings in Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) esophagitis, another opportunistic infection seen in immunocompromised patients. It presents with multiple small, well-defined "punched-out" ulcers in the esophagus, not the white, plaque-like lesions characteristic of Candida albicans. @Neet_pg_bot

CDC-AIDS defining conditions:

  • Candidiasis of the bronchi, trachea, oesophagal or lungs. (Option A)
  • Cryptosporidiosis with diarrhoea (for longer than 1 month)

  • Herpes simplex: chronic ulcers (lasting longer than 1 month); or bronchitis, pneumonitis, or esophagitis (beginning when older than one month)

  • Lymphoma, primary, of brain
  • Mycobacterium avium complex (type of bacterial infection) or M. kansasii, disseminated or extrapulmonary
  • Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia (PCP)
  • Progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy
  • Toxoplasmosis of the brain, beginning when older than one month

Acid-fast bacilli (Option B) are typically associated with infections caused by Mycobacterium species, such as tuberculosis or Mycobacterium avium complex. Their clinical presentation and diagnostic approach differ significantly; diagnosis relies on acid-fast staining of tissue or bodily fluids, rather than endoscopic findings of white esophageal plaques, which are more characteristic of fungal infections like candidiasis.

Branching septate hyphae at a 45-degree angle (Option C) is a hallmark of Aspergillus species, a type of mold that most commonly infects the lungs or sinuses, especially in immunocompromised individuals. Additionally, when Aspergillus does infect mucosal tissues, it does not produce the white plaque-like lesions seen in esophageal candidiasis.

Multinucleated giant cells with intranuclear inclusions (Option D) are classic histological findings in Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) esophagitis, another opportunistic infection seen in immunocompromised patients. It presents with multiple small, well-defined "punched-out" ulcers in the esophagus, not the white, plaque-like lesions characteristic of Candida albicans.

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with a progressively increasing swelling over the tibia along with fever. Radiological examination reveals a Codman triangle and sunburst appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy presents with a progressively increasing swelling over the tibia along with fever. Radiological examination reveals a Codman triangle and sunburst appearance. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Based on the presentation and the radiological findings of codman triangle and sunburst appearance, the most likely diagnosis is Osteosarcoma . Osteosarcoma: It is the most common primary malignant tumour of bone and accounts for approximately 20% of bone cancers. Age distribution: Bimodal. Tumours usually arise in the metaphyseal region of the long bones; almost 50% are near the knee in the distal femur or proximal tibia. Genetic associations: RB gene (most common): 70%. TP53. CDKN2A (also known as INK4a). MDM2 and CDK4. Morphology: Osteosarcomas are bulky, gritty, grey-white tumours that often contain haemorrhage and cystic degeneration. Osteosarcomas demonstrate pleomorphism , large hyperchromatic nuclei , bizarre tumour giant cells , and abundant mitoses. Extensive necrosis and intravascular invasion are also common. Diagnosis of osteosarcoma requires the presence of malignant tumour cells producing unmineralised osteoid or mineralised bone. Osteosarcoma metastasises hematogenously to the lungs, bones, brain, and other sites. X-ray findings of osteosarcoma: Area of irregular destruction in the metaphysis. The cortex overlying the lesion is eroded. Sun-ray or Sun burst appearance (aggressive periostitis): As the tumor grows into the overlying soft tissues new bone is laid down centrifugally along the blood vessels within the tumor. Codman's triangle: Elevation of periosteum by the growing tumor in the form of a triangle Ewing sarcoma (Option B) is the second most common in children and young adults and its radiology shows onion-skin appearance , not Codman triangle or sunburst pattern. Giant cell tumour (Option C) is a benign but locally aggressive tumour characterised by numerous multinucleated osteoclast-type giant cells. It occurs in the third to fifth decades of life. Radiology shows soap bubble appearance , which is lobulated lytic lesions with narrow zones of transition ﻿﻿﻿Chondrosarcoma (Option C) is a malignant cartilage-producing tumour. It is the second most common malignant matrix-producing tumour of the bone and affects individuals usually in their 40s or older . They commonly arise in the axial skeleton, especially the pelvis, shoulder, and ribs. It does not show Codman triangle or sunburst pattern in a X-ray. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which type of pulse is based on the Frank-Starling law?
questions.stemHtml: Which type of pulse is based on the Frank-Starling law?
questions.solution: stomMeta" data-dictid="ea15b7aee31692777181bed9878744">alternans shows alternating strong and weak pulse beats, often seen in severe left ventricular dysfunction. One proposed mechanism involves the Frank-Starling law , where a weak contraction leads to increased end-diastolic volume, boosting the next beat's strength. This cycle repeats, causing alternating pulse amplitudes. Another theory involves abnormal calcium cycling in cardiac myocytes. The Frank-Starling law of the heart describes the relationship between the volume of blood filling the heart (end-diastolic volume) and the force of contraction during the next heartbeat (stroke volume) . Mechanism: Preload: Increased venous return leads to increased end-diastolic volume. Myocardial Stretch: Greater end-diastolic volume stretches the myocardial fibers. Force of Contraction: The stretched fibers generate a more forceful contraction due to the optimal overlap of actin and myosin filaments (length-tension relationship). Incorrect Options: Pulsus bisferiens (Option A): Characterised by a double systolic peak; seen in aortic regurgitation or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy—not related to Frank-Starling. Pulsus paradoxus (Option B): An exaggerated decrease in systolic BP during inspiration, typically seen in cardiac tamponade or severe asthma, not explained by Frank-Starling law. Pulsus parvus (Option D): A small, weak pulse seen in aortic stenosis; related to obstruction , not preload or contractility. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A child presents with petechiae, purpura, and a platelet count of 10,000/µL. Bone marrow examination reveals increased megakaryocytes.Which of the following is the drug of choice (DOC) for this condition?
questions.stemHtml: A child presents with petechiae, purpura, and a platelet count of 10,000/µL. Bone marrow examination reveals increased megakaryocytes.Which of the following is the drug of choice (DOC) for this condition?
questions.solution: ) Explanation This clinical presentation (petechiae, purpura, platelet count of 10,000/µL, and increased megakaryocytes in bone marrow) is characteristic of Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP) , also previously known as Idiopathic Thrombocytopenic Purpura. In ITP, the immune system mistakenly attacks and destroys platelets, leading to a low platelet count. The bone marrow, in an attempt to compensate for the rapid destruction, produces more megakaryocytes (the precursor cells to platelets), which is why their number is increased on bone marrow examination. Bone marrow transplant (Option A ruled out) : This is a very aggressive and high-risk procedure. It is not a first-line treatment for ITP. It might be considered in very rare, refractory cases of severe, chronic ITP that haven't responded to multiple other treatments, but it's far from the drug of choice. Methotrexate (Option B ruled out) : This is an immunosuppressant and chemotherapy agent. While some immunosuppressants might be used in refractory chronic ITP (e.g., rituximab, cyclosporine, azathioprine), methotrexate is not a standard first-line drug of choice for acute severe ITP in children. Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) (Option C) : This is a primary drug of choice for acute, severe ITP, especially when a rapid increase in platelet count is desired due to significant bleeding or very low counts. It's often used alongside or as an alternative to corticosteroids. Aspirin (Option D ruled out) Aspirin is an antiplatelet agent that inhibits platelet function. Giving aspirin to a patient with a critically low platelet count and bleeding (petechiae, purpura) would be highly contraindicated as it would worsen bleeding. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Mitral stenosis murmur corresponds to which wave of ECG?
questions.stemHtml: Mitral stenosis murmur corresponds to which wave of ECG?
questions.solution: a diastolic rumbling murmur that follows the opening snap of the mitral valve. It is best heard at the apex and is associated with left atrial contraction . The P wave on ECG represents atrial depolarization . Since mitral stenosis involves obstruction to left ventricular filling during atrial contraction , the murmur is timed with and follows the P wave . In severe mitral stenosis, a loud first heart sound and presystolic accentuation of the murmur (due to atrial contraction) are commonly observed, directly relating to the P wave . Mitral stenosis (MS) causes left atrial enlargement , which typically appears on ECG as Broad, bifid P waves , especially in lead II → “P mitrale.” P Wave in ECG: Feature Normal P Wave Right Atrial Enlargement (P Pulmonale ) Left Atrial Enlargement (P Mitrale ) Cause Normal atrial depolarization Pulmonary disease Congenital heart disease Tricuspid valve disorders Mitral valve disease Left ventricular failure Amplitude < 2.5 mm > 2.5 mm (in leads II, III, aVF, sometimes V1) May be increased but less prominent than in RAA Duration < 0.12 sec (120 ms) Normal (< 0.12 sec) Prolonged > 0.12 sec (broad P wave) Shape Smooth, upright Tall, peaked, narrow Notched/bifid ("M"-shaped) in lead II Lead II Appearance Smooth and positive Tall, peaked P wave Notched/bifid P wave Lead V1 Appearance Biphasic (small negative) Deep P wave Biphasic with prominent, prolonged negative terminal @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding breastfeeding technique is/are incorrect? A) The infant’s lower lip should be inverted during latching B) The infant’s cheeks should appear full during effective suckling C) A greater portion of areola should be covered above the breast than below D) The infant’s chin should make contact with the breast during feeding
questions.stemHtml:
Which of the following statements regarding breastfeeding technique is/are incorrect?
A) The infant’s lower lip should be inverted during latching
B) The infant’s cheeks should appear full during effective suckling
C) A greater portion of areola should be covered above the breast than below
D) The infant’s chin should make contact with the breast during feeding
questions.solution: ong>Explanation A) The infant's lower lip should be inverted during latching: This statement is incorrect. For a proper latch, the infant's lower lip should be everted (flanged outwards), not inverted. An inverted lower lip indicates a shallow latch and can lead to nipple pain for the mother and inadequate milk transfer for the baby. B) The infant's cheeks should appear full during effective suckling: This statement is correct. When an infant is effectively suckling and getting milk, their cheeks should appear full and rounded, indicating that their mouth is well-filled with breast tissue and they are creating good suction. Dimpling of the cheeks often suggests a shallow latch or ineffective suckling. C) A greater portion of areola should be covered above the breast than below: This statement is incorrect. For an effective latch, a greater portion of the areola should be covered BELOW the nipple than above it. This allows the infant to take in more breast tissue from the underside, which is crucial for compressing the milk ducts and extracting milk efficiently. D) The infant's chin should make contact with the breast during feeding: This statement is correct. The infant's chin should be tucked into the breast, making good contact. This position helps the baby to open their mouth wide and take in a good amount of breast tissue, facilitating a deep and effective latch. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the mechanism of breast milk jaundice?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best explains the mechanism of breast milk jaundice?

options.label: A
options.text: Increased bilirubin production due to red blood cell breakdown

options.label: B
options.text: Inhibition of bilirubin conjugation by substances such as non-esterified fatty acids and beta-glucuronidase, in breast milk

options.label: C
options.text: Hepatocellular injury caused by maternal hormones

questions.answerText: Inhibition of bilirubin conjugation by substances such as non-esterified fatty acids and beta-glucuronidase, in breast milk
questions.solution: -glucuronidase, in breast milk Explanation Breast milk jaundice is a type of prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that typically appears after the first week of life in otherwise healthy, exclusively breastfed infants. The exact mechanism is not fully understood, but it's believed that certain factors in breast milk interfere with the normal processing and excretion of bilirubin. Beta-glucuronidase is an enzyme present in breast milk that can deconjugate bilirubin in the infant's intestine. This deconjugated bilirubin can then be reabsorbed into the bloodstream (enterohepatic circulation), leading to elevated bilirubin levels. Non-esterified fatty acids (also called free fatty acids), which are released from breast milk triglycerides by the action of lipase, can also inhibit the enzyme in the liver (glucuronyl transferase) responsible for conjugating bilirubin. Conjugation is a crucial step for bilirubin to be excreted from the body. Other Options ruled out Increased bilirubin production due to red blood cell breakdown (Option A ruled out) : This is the primary mechanism for physiologic jaundice (which occurs in the first few days of life) and hemolytic jaundice (due to conditions like ABO incompatibility). While newborns naturally have increased RBC breakdown, breast milk jaundice specifically refers to the prolonged jaundice due to breast milk factors, not primarily increased production. Hepatocellular injury caused by maternal hormones (Option C ruled out) : While some early theories suggested certain maternal hormones (like pregnane-3α,20β-diol) in breast milk might play a role, this mechanism is not as strongly supported or understood as the role of beta-glucuronidase and free fatty acids. Hepatocellular injury is also not the defining feature of breast milk jaundice. Decreased intestinal absorption of bilirubin (Option D ruled out) : This is the opposite of what happens. Breast milk jaundice is thought to involve increased enterohepatic circulation, meaning more bilirubin is reabsorbed from the intestine, not less. @Neet_pg_bot

-glucuronidase, in breast milk

Explanation

  • Breast milk jaundice is a type of prolonged unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia that typically appears after the first week of life in otherwise healthy, exclusively breastfed infants.
  • The exact mechanism is not fully understood, but it's believed that certain factors in breast milk interfere with the normal processing and excretion of bilirubin.
  • Beta-glucuronidase is an enzyme present in breast milk that can deconjugate bilirubin in the infant's intestine. This deconjugated bilirubin can then be reabsorbed into the bloodstream (enterohepatic circulation), leading to elevated bilirubin levels.
  • Non-esterified fatty acids (also called free fatty acids), which are released from breast milk triglycerides by the action of lipase, can also inhibit the enzyme in the liver (glucuronyl transferase) responsible for conjugating bilirubin. Conjugation is a crucial step for bilirubin to be excreted from the body.

Other Options ruled out

  • Increased bilirubin production due to red blood cell breakdown(Option A ruled out): This is the primary mechanism for physiologic jaundice (which occurs in the first few days of life) and hemolytic jaundice (due to conditions like ABO incompatibility). While newborns naturally have increased RBC breakdown, breast milk jaundice specifically refers to the prolonged jaundice due to breast milk factors, not primarily increased production.
  • Hepatocellular injury caused by maternal hormones(Option C ruled out): While some early theories suggested certain maternal hormones (like pregnane-3α,20β-diol) in breast milk might play a role, this mechanism is not as strongly supported or understood as the role of beta-glucuronidase and free fatty acids. Hepatocellular injury is also not the defining feature of breast milk jaundice.
  • Decreased intestinal absorption of bilirubin(Option D ruled out): This is the opposite of what happens. Breast milk jaundice is thought to involve increased enterohepatic circulation, meaning more bilirubin is reabsorbed from the intestine, not less.

Which among the following are incorrect about tension pneumothorax?
	Occurs due to improper dressing of open wound

questions.solution: atements 2 and 3 are incorrect while 1 and 4 are correct. A tension pneumothorax develops when a ‘one-way valve’ air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall. Open (sucking) chest wounds can act as a one-way valve when improperly dressed. Air enters during inspiration but cannot exit during expiration, causing a valve mechanism , leading to tension pneumothorax . (Statement 1) High cervical spinal injuries may result in diaphragmatic paralysis or respiratory failure, predisposing to pneumothorax due to barotrauma from mechanical ventilation or reduced clearance. Though indirect, spinal injury can be associated with tension pneumothorax. (Statement 4) TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX Pathophysiology D/t ‘one-way valve’ air leaks from the lung or chest wall. Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any escape, collapsing and compressing the affected lung. The mediastinum shifts to the opposite side, reducing venous return and compressing the opposite lung, leading to decreased cardiac output and function. This can result in sudden death. Causes Penetrating Chest Trauma. Blunt Chest Trauma with parenchymal lung injury and persistent air leak. (Statement 2) Iatrogenic Lung Injury (e.g., central venepuncture) Mechanical Positive-Pressure Ventilation. (Statement 3) Clinical Features Tachypnea and Tachycardia Hyper-resonance and Decreased/Absent Breath Sounds Resonant Percussion with severe mediastinal/tracheal shift Cyanosis and Hypotension Chest Pain Distended Neck Veins Emergency Management Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confirmation. Safe Triangle Boundaries : Posterior: Latissimus dorsi Anterior: Lateral border of the pectoralis major Inferior: A line drawn perpendicularly from the nipple to the back, just anterior to the mid-axillary line. In critical situations, a finger thoracostomy can be done in the same location. Nasal Oxygen for support. Intercostal Tube Placement (ICT) once stable and confirmed by chest X-ray. questions.solutionHtml:
atements 2 and 3 are incorrect while 1 and 4 are correct.
  • A tension pneumothorax develops when a ‘one-way valve’ air leak occurs either from the lung or through the chest wall.
  • Open (sucking) chest wounds can act as a one-way valve when improperly dressed. Air enters during inspiration but cannot exit during expiration, causing a valve mechanism, leading to tension pneumothorax. (Statement 1)
  • High cervical spinal injuries may result in diaphragmatic paralysis or respiratory failure, predisposing to pneumothorax due to barotrauma from mechanical ventilation or reduced clearance. Though indirect, spinal injury can be associated with tension pneumothorax. (Statement 4)

 

TENSION PNEUMOTHORAX

Pathophysiology
  • D/t ‘one-way valve’ air leaks from the lung or chest wall.
  • Air is sucked into the thoracic cavity without any escape, collapsing and compressing the affected lung.
  • The mediastinum shifts to the opposite side, reducing venous return and compressing the opposite lung, leading to decreased cardiac output and function. This can result in sudden death.

Causes
  • Penetrating Chest Trauma.
  • Blunt Chest Trauma with parenchymal lung injury and persistent air leak. (Statement 2)
  • Iatrogenic Lung Injury (e.g., central venepuncture)
  • Mechanical Positive-Pressure Ventilation. (Statement 3)

Clinical Features
  • Tachypnea and Tachycardia
  • Hyper-resonance and Decreased/Absent Breath Sounds
  • Resonant Percussion with severe mediastinal/tracheal shift
  • Cyanosis and Hypotension
  • Chest Pain
  • Distended Neck Veins

Emergency Management
  • Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis, and treatment should never be delayed by waiting for radiological confirmation.
  • Immediate Thoracocentesis (needle): Wide bore needle (typically a 20- or 22-gauge) in the 5th intercostal space in the safety triangle.
  • Decompression should be performed in the "safe triangle."
  • Safe Triangle Boundaries:
    • Posterior: Latissimus dorsi
    • Anterior: Lateral border of the pectoralis major
    • Inferior: A line drawn perpendicularly from the nipple to the back, just anterior to the mid-axillary line.

  • In critical situations, a finger thoracostomy can be done in the same location.
  • Nasal Oxygen for support.
  • Intercostal Tube Placement (ICT) once stable and confirmed by chest X-ray.

Additional Care

  • Antibiotics and analgesics for treatment.
  • Ventilator Support with IPPV in severe cases.

questions.stem: All of the following is a contraindication to Breast Conservation surgery except ?
questions.stemHtml: All of the following is a contraindication to Breast Conservation surgery except ?

options.label: A
options.text: Previous history of radiation to the chest

options.label: D
options.text: Persistent positive margins even after resection

questions.solution: Breast conservation surgery (BCS), also known as lumpectomy or wide local excision (WLE), is contraindicated in certain conditions where it may compromise oncological safety or cosmetic outcomes. BCS is feasible if the tumor is confined to a single quadrant and is aimed at removing the tumour along with a 1-cm margin of normal breast tissue. All patients with BCS receive radiotherapy. BCS together with radiotherapy is called breast conservation therapy (BCT): BCS + RT = BCT BCS is avoided in patients with: Multicentric tumour Diffuse microcalcifications on a mammogram Large tumour-to-breast ratio Two times positive surgical margins after re-excision History of previous breast or chest wall radiation Systemic lupus erythematosus or other collagen vascular disease (these patients have a high risk of a radiation reaction), or ankylosing spondylitis Severe orthopnea (as the patient cannot lie on the radiation table) Previous history of radiation to the chest (Option A) Prior radiation to the chest (e.g., for Hodgkin’s lymphoma) increases the risk of radiation-induced toxicity and poor wound healing, making BCS unsafe. Scleroderma (Option C) Scleroderma (a connective tissue disorder) impairs wound healing and increases radiation toxicity, making BCS + radiotherapy risky. Persistent positive margins even after resection (Option D) Patients with involved margins will have to undergo a revision of margins called a ‘cavity shave’. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Breast conservation surgery (BCS), also known as lumpectomy or wide local excision (WLE), is contraindicated in certain conditions where it may compromise oncological safety or cosmetic outcomes. BCS is feasible if the tumor is confined to a single quadrant and is aimed at removing the tumour along with a 1-cm margin of normal breast tissue. All patients with BCS receive radiotherapy. BCS together with radiotherapy is called breast conservation therapy (BCT): BCS + RT = BCT

BCS is avoided in patients with:

  1. Multicentric tumour
  2. Diffuse microcalcifications on a mammogram
  3. Large tumour-to-breast ratio
  4. Two times positive surgical margins after re-excision
  5. History of previous breast or chest wall radiation
  6. Systemic lupus erythematosus or other collagen vascular disease (these patients have a high risk of a radiation reaction), or ankylosing spondylitis
  7. Severe orthopnea (as the patient cannot lie on the radiation table)

Previous history of radiation to the chest (Option A) Prior radiation to the chest (e.g., for Hodgkin’s lymphoma) increases the risk of radiation-induced toxicity and poor wound healing, making BCS unsafe.

Scleroderma (Option C) Scleroderma (a connective tissue disorder) impairs wound healing and increases radiation toxicity, making BCS + radiotherapy risky.

Persistent positive margins even after resection (Option D) Patients with involved margins will have to undergo a revision of margins called a ‘cavity shave’.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the development of hyponatremia in a hypovolemic patient with diarrhea?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best explains the development of hyponatremia in a hypovolemic patient with diarrhea?

options.label: A
options.text: Decreased reabsorption of sodium from kidney

options.label: D
options.text: Decreased sodium absorption from the intestine

questions.solution: Hyponatremia in a hypovolemic patient with diarrhea is a common and important clinical scenario. Let's analyze the options: a. Decreased reabsorption of sodium from kidney: In hypovolemia, the body's compensatory mechanisms (like the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system) actually increase sodium reabsorption from the kidney to try and conserve volume. So, this is unlikely to be the primary cause of hyponatremia in this context. b. Decreased secretion of aldosterone: Aldosterone secretion is increased in hypovolemia as part of the body's attempt to conserve sodium and water. Decreased aldosterone would lead to sodium loss , but it's not the normal response to hypovolemia. c. Non-osmotic release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH): This is the most likely and best explanation. In significant hypovolemia (even if plasma osmolality is normal or low), the body prioritizes maintaining circulating volume. This triggers a non-osmotic release of ADH from the posterior pituitary. This ADH then acts on the kidneys to increase water reabsorption, leading to dilution of existing sodium and thus hyponatremia. Despite having diarrhea (which causes loss of both water and electrolytes), if the patient is rehydrated with hypotonic fluids (e.g., plain water) or if the ADH-induced water retention is significant, hyponatremia can develop. d. Decreased sodium absorption from the intestine: Diarrhea primarily involves increased fluid and electrolyte loss from the intestine, not necessarily decreased absorption of sodium (though absorption can be impaired). While the loss of sodium contributes to the overall electrolyte imbalance, the dilutional aspect caused by inappropriate water retention is critical for hyponatremia in the setting of hypovolemia and ADH release. Therefore, the best explanation for the development of hyponatremia in a hypovolemic patient with diarrhea is c. Non-osmotic release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH). The body's overwhelming drive to restore blood volume overrides the normal osmotic regulation of ADH, leading to excessive water retention relative to sodium. @Neet_pg_bot

  • b. Decreased secretion of aldosterone: Aldosterone secretion is increased in hypovolemia as part of the body's attempt to conserve sodium and water. Decreased aldosterone would lead to sodium loss, but it's not the normal response to hypovolemia.
     
  • c. Non-osmotic release of antidiuretic hormone (ADH): This is the most likely and best explanation. In significant hypovolemia (even if plasma osmolality is normal or low), the body prioritizes maintaining circulating volume. This triggers a non-osmotic release of ADH from the posterior pituitary. This ADH then acts on the kidneys to increase water reabsorption, leading to dilution of existing sodium and thus hyponatremia. Despite having diarrhea (which causes loss of both water and electrolytes), if the patient is rehydrated with hypotonic fluids (e.g., plain water) or if the ADH-induced water retention is significant, hyponatremia can develop.
     
  • d. Decreased sodium absorption from the intestine: Diarrhea primarily involves increased fluid and electrolyte loss from the intestine, not necessarily decreased absorption of sodium (though absorption can be impaired). While the loss of sodium contributes to the overall electrolyte imbalance, the dilutional aspect caused by inappropriate water retention is critical for hyponatremia in the setting of hypovolemia and ADH release.

questions.stem: Caspase-1 is primarily involved in which type of programmed cell death?
questions.stemHtml: Caspase-1 is primarily involved in which type of programmed cell death?
questions.solution: Caspase-1 plays a central role in Pyroptosis , a form of programmed cell death associated with inflammation. It is a form of apoptosis in which there is release of the fever-inducing cytokine IL-1. Microbial products entering infected cells are recognized by cytoplasmic receptors, activating the multiprotein complex inflammasome. This complex activates caspase 1 which converts the inactive IL-1 to active IL-1, causing fever, inflammation and leucocyte recruitment. (Option B) Pyroptosis is the mechanism by which some microbes cause the death of infected cells and trigger local inflammation. Apoptosis (Option A) is a controlled, non-inflammatory cell death involving caspases-8, -9, -3, and -7, but not caspase-1, and serves to remove damaged cells without triggering an immune response. Necroptosis (Option C) is a programmed inflammatory cell death triggered when apoptosis is blocked, involving RIPK1, RIPK3, and MLKL—but not caspase-1, distinguishing it from pyroptosis. Necrosis (Option D) is an uncontrolled, non-programmed cell death due to injury (e.g., trauma or ischemia), causing inflammation without involving caspases, including caspase-1. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is an example of a feed-forward mechanism?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is an example of a feed-forward mechanism?

options.label: B
options.text: Increase in heart rate on standing from supine position

options.label: C
options.text: Increased cardiac output in response to anemia

questions.solution: Correct Answer- Option D) Temperature Regulation Feedforward Description: Anticipates a change and initiates responses before the change fully occurs. Examples: Cephalic phase of gastric secretion (e.g., salivating when you see food). Temperature regulation (e.g., shivering before body temperature drops significantly). Anxiety leading to tachycardia (heart rate increase). Vasoconstriction in response to cooling: Feedforward Component: As discussed previously, the anticipation of a core temperature drop based on skin cooling provides a crucial feedforward element, allowing for a rapid, preemptive response. Increase in heart rate on standing from a supine position: Feedforward Component: The combined effect of increased heart rate, contractility, and vasoconstriction helps to restore blood pressure to near normal levels, maintaining adequate blood flow to the brain. Increased cardiac output in response to anemia: Feedforward Component: The increased cardiac output (achieved through increased heart rate, stroke volume, and reduced afterload) attempts to deliver more blood, and thus more oxygen, to the oxygen-deprived tissues. This is a compensatory mechanism to maintain oxygen delivery despite the reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Answer- Option D) Temperature Regulation

Feedforward

  • Description: Anticipates a change and initiates responses before the change fully occurs.
  • Examples:
    • Cephalic phase of gastric secretion (e.g., salivating when you see food).
    • Temperature regulation (e.g., shivering before body temperature drops significantly).
    • Anxiety leading to tachycardia (heart rate increase).

 

Vasoconstriction in response to cooling:
Feedforward Component: As discussed previously, the anticipation of a core temperature drop based on skin cooling provides a crucial feedforward element, allowing for a rapid, preemptive response.

 

Increase in heart rate on standing from a supine position:
Feedforward Component: The combined effect of increased heart rate, contractility, and vasoconstriction helps to restore blood pressure to near normal levels, maintaining adequate blood flow to the brain.

 

Increased cardiac output in response to anemia:
Feedforward Component: The increased cardiac output (achieved through increased heart rate, stroke volume, and reduced afterload) attempts to deliver more blood, and thus more oxygen, to the oxygen-deprived tissues. This is a compensatory mechanism to maintain oxygen delivery despite the reduced oxygen-carrying capacity of the blood.

questions.stem: Cancer cells take up excess glucose because?
questions.stemHtml: Cancer cells take up excess glucose because?

options.label: A
options.text: Lactate is produced even in the presence of Oxygen

questions.answerText: Lactate is produced even in the presence of Oxygen
questions.solution: /strong> Cancer cells demonstrate the Warburg Effect by favoring the conversion of glucose to lactate even in the presence of adequate oxygen, a process known as aerobic glycolysis. The phenomenon in cancer cells where, even in the presence of oxygen, glucose is primarily converted to lactate through aerobic glycolysis. (Option A) Significance: This allows faster ATP production and provides intermediates for neoplastic cell growth and multiplication. It increases NADPH production, protecting neoplastic cells from oxidative stress. High NADH/NAD ratio (Option B): Although the NADH/NAD⁺ balance affects cellular metabolism, it is not the primary reason cancer cells take up excess glucose. The Warburg effect drives increased glucose uptake regardless of NADH levels. High GLUT2 (Option C): GLUT2 is a glucose transporter mainly found in liver, pancreatic beta cells, and kidney, not commonly involved in cancer cell glucose uptake. Cancer cells typically overexpress GLUT1 or other transporters to increase glucose intake. Absence of Oxygen (Option D): While low oxygen (hypoxia) can stimulate glucose uptake, many cancer cells continue to produce lactate and consume large amounts of glucose even when oxygen is plentiful, which is the hallmark of aerobic glycolysis, not simply hypoxia-induced metabolism. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
/strong>

Cancer cells demonstrate the Warburg Effect by favoring the conversion of glucose to lactate even in the presence of adequate oxygen, a process known as aerobic glycolysis.

  • The phenomenon in cancer cells where, even in the presence of oxygen, glucose is primarily converted to lactate through aerobic glycolysis. (Option A)
  • Significance:
    • This allows faster ATP production and provides intermediates for neoplastic cell growth and multiplication.
    • It increases NADPH production, protecting neoplastic cells from oxidative stress.

 

High NADH/NAD ratio (Option B): Although the NADH/NAD⁺ balance affects cellular metabolism, it is not the primary reason cancer cells take up excess glucose. The Warburg effect drives increased glucose uptake regardless of NADH levels.
 

High GLUT2 (Option C): GLUT2 is a glucose transporter mainly found in liver, pancreatic beta cells, and kidney, not commonly involved in cancer cell glucose uptake. Cancer cells typically overexpress GLUT1 or other transporters to increase glucose intake.
 

Absence of Oxygen (Option D): While low oxygen (hypoxia) can stimulate glucose uptake, many cancer cells continue to produce lactate and consume large amounts of glucose even when oxygen is plentiful, which is the hallmark of aerobic glycolysis, not simply hypoxia-induced metabolism.
