questions.stem: A male presents with lesions and a history of unprotected sexual intercourse a few months ago. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A male presents with lesions and a history of unprotected sexual intercourse a few months ago. What is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.solution: ong> The lesions depicted in the image, along with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse, suggest a diagnosis of Secondary Syphilis , which is best confirmed through serological testing. It is the second stage of syphilis, which occurs if primary syphilis is left untreated. It presents a few weeks to several months after the initial chancre has healed. It is marked by systemic manifestations and can affect multiple organ systems. Clinical Features: Diffuse, non-pruritic rash, often reddish-brown macules or papules, that is polymorphous and non-vesicular . Mucous membrane lesions, such as condylomata lata , appear in moist areas like the oral cavity and genitals and are highly infectious. Oral signs may include mucous patches or snail track ulcers. “Moth-eaten" alopecia: A patchy, non-scarring hair loss. Buschke-Ollendorff sign: Deep tenderness over lesions. Painless generalized lymphadenopathy (especially epitrochlear nodes)l. Systemic symptoms include fever, malaise, and fatigue, with rare cases showing neurological or ocular involvement. Diagnosis : By serological testing: (Option A) Non-Treponemal Tests : RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) and VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) are used for screening. These tests detect nonspecific antibodies and can be positive in other conditions. Treponemal Tests : FTA-ABS (Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption) confirms the diagnosis by detecting antibodies specific to Treponema pallidum. Treatment: Standard treatment: Benzathine penicillin G . Dosage: 2.4 million units intramuscularly in a single dose. For those allergic to penicillin, alternatives such as doxycycline or tetracycline can be used. Complications : If left untreated, secondary syphilis can progress to the latent stage and eventually tertiary syphilis, which can lead to serious complications, including cardiovascular, neurological, and systemic damage. Incorrect Options: Tzanck smear (Option B) is a diagnostic test primarily used for identifying infections caused by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella-Zoster Virus. It involves examining cells scraped from a lesion under a microscope. However, this test has no role in diagnosing syphilis, as it does not detect Treponema pallidum, the bacterium responsible for the disease. KOH preparation (Option C) is commonly employed to diagnose superficial fungal infections such as dermatophytosis or candidiasis. A sample from the skin, hair, or nails is treated with potassium hydroxide, which dissolves keratin and allows for the visualization of fungal elements under a microscope. Since syphilis is a bacterial infection, this test is irrelevant in its diagnosis. Biopsy (Option D) is used to evaluate suspicious skin lesions when the diagnosis is unclear, and it can sometimes reveal histopathological features suggestive of syphilis. It is invasive and nonspecific, whereas serological tests are more sensitive, specific, and the preferred method for diagnosing secondary syphilis. @Neet_pg_bot

The lesions depicted in the image, along with a history of unprotected sexual intercourse, suggest a diagnosis of Secondary Syphilis, which is best confirmed through serological testing.

  • It is the second stage of syphilis, which occurs if primary syphilis is left untreated.
  • It presents a few weeks to several months after the initial chancre has healed.
  • It is marked by systemic manifestations and can affect multiple organ systems.
  • Clinical Features:
    • Diffuse, non-pruritic rash, often reddish-brown macules or papules, that is polymorphous and non-vesicular.
    • Mucous membrane lesions, such as condylomata lata, appear in moist areas like the oral cavity and genitals and are highly infectious.
    • Oral signs may include mucous patches or snail track ulcers.
    • “Moth-eaten" alopecia: A patchy, non-scarring hair loss.
    • Buschke-Ollendorff sign: Deep tenderness over lesions.
    • Painless generalized lymphadenopathy (especially epitrochlear nodes)l.
    • Systemic symptoms include fever, malaise, and fatigue, with rare cases showing neurological or ocular involvement.
  • Diagnosis: By serological testing: (Option A)
    • Non-Treponemal Tests:
      • RPR (Rapid Plasma Reagin) and VDRL (Venereal Disease Research Laboratory) are used for screening.
      • These tests detect nonspecific antibodies and can be positive in other conditions.
    • Treponemal Tests:
      • FTA-ABS (Fluorescent Treponemal Antibody Absorption) confirms the diagnosis by detecting antibodies specific to Treponema pallidum.
  • Treatment:
    • Standard treatment: Benzathine penicillin G.
    • Dosage: 2.4 million units intramuscularly in a single dose.
    • For those allergic to penicillin, alternatives such as doxycycline or tetracycline can be used.
  • Complications: If left untreated, secondary syphilis can progress to the latent stage and eventually tertiary syphilis, which can lead to serious complications, including cardiovascular, neurological, and systemic damage.

Incorrect Options:

Tzanck smear (Option B) is a diagnostic test primarily used for identifying infections caused by Herpes Simplex Virus (HSV) and Varicella-Zoster Virus. It involves examining cells scraped from a lesion under a microscope. However, this test has no role in diagnosing syphilis, as it does not detect Treponema pallidum, the bacterium responsible for the disease.

KOH preparation (Option C) is commonly employed to diagnose superficial fungal infections such as dermatophytosis or candidiasis. A sample from the skin, hair, or nails is treated with potassium hydroxide, which dissolves keratin and allows for the visualization of fungal elements under a microscope. Since syphilis is a bacterial infection, this test is irrelevant in its diagnosis.

Biopsy (Option D) is used to evaluate suspicious skin lesions when the diagnosis is unclear, and it can sometimes reveal histopathological features suggestive of syphilis. It is invasive and nonspecific, whereas serological tests are more sensitive, specific, and the preferred method for diagnosing secondary syphilis.

ntone (Thiopental) is a barbiturate used for induction of anesthesia. It is classified as an ultrashort-acting agent, and this characteristic is due to its rapid redistribution

  • Thiopental sodium has a rapid onset due to its high lipid solubility and high nonionized fraction, allowing for quick redistribution from the bloodstream to the brain.

    • Thiopentone Sodium:

    • Use: Intravenous induction agent.

    • Prepared concentration: 2.5% solution

    • Form: Yellowish-white crystalline powder or pale greenish hygroscopic powder

    • Odor: Garlic-like odor.

    • Formulation: Thiopental sodium for injection is a sterile mixture of thiopental sodium and anhydrous sodium carbonate (buffer).

    • Should not be reconstituted with lactated Ringer’s solution or mixed with acidic solutions, as this reduces alkalinity and may cause precipitation of the drug as free acid.

    • pH: 11

    • Melting Point: The free acid (thiopental) melts at 158–160°C.

    • Solubility:

      • Water: Soluble in 1.5 parts of water at 20°C.

      • Alcohol: Partially soluble.

      • Insoluble: Practically insoluble in ether, benzene, and petroleum ether.

    • Pharmacokinetics:

      • Higher potency.

      • Rapid onset and short duration of action.

      • Dose: 3-6 mg/kg

      • Duration of onset: 15-20 seconds

      • Duration of action: 6-10 minutes

      • Elimination T1/2: 12 hours (Option D)

      • Exhibits first-order kinetics.

      • Unique property: Duration of induction dose is determined by redistribution.

      • Metabolism: Liver (plays a role in elimination, not in the rapid offset of action) (Option B)

      • Excretion site: Kidney, (renal excretion is also slow and doesn't affect the immediate duration of action) (Option C)

questions.stemHtml: Which of the following vaccines is contraindicated in a patient diagnosed with Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID)?
questions.solution: tient with SCID. Explanation Severe Combined Immunodeficiency (SCID) is a life-threatening primary immunodeficiency characterized by a severe defect in both cellular (T-cell) and humoral (B-cell, indirectly) immunity. Patients with SCID are highly susceptible to infections. The general rule for vaccinating immunocompromised individuals, especially those with severe immunodeficiencies like SCID, is to avoid live-attenuated vaccines. Live-attenuated vaccines contain weakened forms of the virus or bacteria, which can replicate in the body and, in a severely immunocompromised person, can cause the full-blown disease rather than a protective immune response. Other options ruled out Hepatitis B (Option A ruled out) : This is an inactivated (killed) vaccine. Inactivated vaccines do not contain live pathogens and are generally safe for immunocompromised individuals, although their immune response might be blunted. Tetanus, Diphtheria, and Pertussis (Tdap) (Option B ruled out) : This is a toxoid and inactivated vaccine (diphtheria and tetanus toxoids, and inactivated pertussis components). It is safe for immunocompromised individuals. Inactivated Poliovirus (IPV) (Option C ruled out) : As the name suggests, this is an inactivated (killed) vaccine. It is safe for immunocompromised individuals. (Note: The Oral Polio Vaccine (OPV) is a live-attenuated vaccine and would be contraindicated). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: ropharyngeal dysphagia is common due to impaired coordination of swallowing muscles. This leads to aspiration of food, liquids, and saliva, resulting in recurrent pneumonitis and long-term complications like bronchiectasis . PEG (Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy) tube helps bypass the oropharyngeal route for nutrition, reducing the risk of aspiration pneumonia and supporting nutritional status. It serves as a long-term management strategy that directly addresses the underlying cause—oropharyngeal dysfunction and aspiration. Incorrect Options: High-frequency chest wall oscillation therapy (Option A) is useful in conditions like cystic fibrosis or bronchiectasis to help clear mucus, but it does not address aspiration or dysphagia, which are the primary issues in this patient. questions.solution: a solid adnexal mass, elevated CA-125, and chronic vague symptoms strongly points to serous ovarian tumor. Types of Epithelial Ovarian Tumor: Type of Epithelial Ovarian Tumor Characteristics Clinical Presentation Serous Tumors Serous Cystadenoma: Benign, unilateral, cystic spaces with serous epithelium. Large cystic mass, unilateral. Serous Cystadenocarcinoma: Malignant, often bilateral, cystic and solid components. Bilateral involvement in 30%, elevated CA-125. Mucinous Tumors Mucinous Cystadenoma: Benign, unilateral, filled with mucinous fluid. Large, unilateral mass. Mucinous Cystadenocarcinoma: Malignant, unilateral, mucinous epithelial lining. May rupture and spread to the peritoneum. Endometrioid Tumors (Option C ruled out) Endometrioid Carcinoma: Arises from endometrial-like tissue, solid and cystic. Solid and cystic components, associated with endometriosis. Clear Cell Tumors Clear Cell Carcinoma: Clear cytoplasm due to glycogen accumulation. Advanced stage, associated with endometriosis. Brenner Tumors (Transitional Cell) Brenner Tumor: Transitional epithelial cells resembling urinary tract epithelium. Rare, usually benign. Mucinous ovarian tumor (Option B) typically presents as a large, unilateral, multiloculated cystic mass and is less commonly associated with peritoneal spread or omental caking. CA-125 elevation is not as prominent unless the disease is advanced, and it lacks the classic imaging and spread pattern seen in serous carcinoma. Granulosa cell tumors (Option D) are sex cord-stromal tumors that secrete estrogen and often cause hormonal symptoms like abnormal uterine bleeding; they rarely cause ascites or omental caking, and CA-125 is typically not elevated. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old chronic smoker presents with complaints of dyspnea. Pulmonary function tests reveal an FEV1/FVC ratio of 65% and an RV/TLC ratio of 141%. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathophysiology?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old chronic smoker presents with complaints of dyspnea. Pulmonary function tests reveal an FEV1/FVC ratio of 65% and an RV/TLC ratio of 141%. Which of the following best describes the underlying pathophysiology?

options.label: A
options.text: Air trapping with hyperinflation of lungs

questions.answerText: Air trapping with hyperinflation of lungs
questions.solution: data-dictid="c92aa64edb16927771867805a38cc6">dyspnea and Obstructive pattern on PFTs, this presentation is most consistent with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) , especially emphysema , which is characterized by destruction of alveolar walls, air trapping, and lung hyperinflation. Smoking leads to inflammation and destruction of elastic fibers in the lungs, resulting in reduced airway recoil, premature airway closure, and gas trapping, which are hallmarks of emphysema. Pathogenesis of COPD Risk Factors Cigarette Smoking : Primary risk, correlates with amount and duration. Environmental Factors : Indoor air pollution (e.g., biomass fuel use in confined spaces). Occupational exposures (e.g., coal dust, silica, cadmium). Developmental Factors : Low birth weight and impaired lung growth from infections or maternal smoking. Infections : Recurrent infections accelerate lung decline. Persistent adenovirus may alter inflammatory responses, leading to damage. Genetic Factors : Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency . (Option B ruled out) Airway hyper-reactivity . Components of COPD Pulmonary Components Description Mucus hypersecretion Enlargement of mucus glands and goblet cells → chronic bronchitis (cough + sputum for ≥3 months/year). Emphysema Alveolar destruction by proteases and oxidants → permanent enlargement of distal airspaces. Airflow Limitation Loss of elastic tissue + inflammation → premature airway closure, gas trapping, and hyperinflation. This is the primary mechanism for the airflow limitation. Pulmonary vascular remodeling Structural changes in pulmonary vessels.eventually causing PAH. Systemic Components Description Weight Loss Altered fat metabolism. Skeletal Muscle Dysfunction Muscle impairment reduces physical capacity. Peripheral Edema Impaired kidney function → salt and water retention. Osteoporosis Decreased bone density. Increased Inflammatory Markers Elevated systemic inflammation contributes to complications. Incorrect Options: Decreased lung compliance (Option B): Seen in restrictive lung diseases (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis). COPD/emphysema features increased, not decreased, compliance due to alveolar wall destruction. Restrictive lung disease (Option C): Would show normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio and decreased lung volumes, not increased RV/TLC. Increased lung compliance (Option D): True for emphysema, but A (air trapping with hyperinflation) better encapsulates the specific pathophysiologic hallmark presented in this question. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Smoking leads to inflammation and destruction of elastic fibers in the lungs, resulting in reduced airway recoil, premature airway closure, and gas trapping, which are hallmarks of emphysema.

    • Pathogenesis of COPD

    Risk Factors

    • Cigarette Smoking: Primary risk, correlates with amount and duration.
    • Environmental Factors:
      • Indoor air pollution (e.g., biomass fuel use in confined spaces).
      • Occupational exposures (e.g., coal dust, silica, cadmium).
    • Developmental Factors:
      • Low birth weight and impaired lung growth from infections or maternal smoking.
    • Infections:
      • Recurrent infections accelerate lung decline.
      • Persistent adenovirus may alter inflammatory responses, leading to damage.
    • Genetic Factors:
      • Alpha-1 antitrypsin deficiency. (Option B ruled out)
      • Airway hyper-reactivity.

    Components of COPD

    Pulmonary Components

    Description

    Mucus hypersecretion

    Enlargement of mucus glands and goblet cells → chronic bronchitis (cough + sputum for ≥3 months/year).

    Emphysema

    Alveolar destruction by proteases and oxidants → permanent enlargement of distal airspaces.

    Airflow Limitation

    Loss of elastic tissue + inflammation → premature airway closure, gas trapping, and hyperinflation.

    This is the primary mechanism for the airflow limitation.

    Pulmonary vascular remodeling

    Structural changes in pulmonary vessels.eventually causing PAH.

     

    Systemic Components

    Description

    Weight Loss

    Altered fat metabolism.

    Skeletal Muscle Dysfunction

    Muscle impairment reduces physical capacity.

    Peripheral Edema

    Impaired kidney function → salt and water retention.

    Osteoporosis

    Decreased bone density.

    Increased Inflammatory Markers

    Elevated systemic inflammation contributes to complications.

    Incorrect Options:

    Decreased lung compliance (Option B): Seen in restrictive lung diseases (e.g., pulmonary fibrosis). COPD/emphysema features increased, not decreased, compliance due to alveolar wall destruction.

    Restrictive lung disease (Option C): Would show normal or increased FEV1/FVC ratio and decreased lung volumes, not increased RV/TLC.

    Increased lung compliance (Option D): True for emphysema, but A (air trapping with hyperinflation) better encapsulates the specific pathophysiologic hallmark presented in this question.

questions.stem: Which of the following best defines blindness ?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following best defines blindness ?

options.label: A
options.text: Visual acuity less than 6/60 in the better eye

options.label: B
options.text: Visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye after best possible correction

options.label: C
options.text: Visual field less than 10 degrees from fixation in the better eye

options.label: D
options.text: Inability to perceive light in both eyes

questions.answerText: Visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye after best possible correction
questions.solution: Correct Option B -Visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye after best possible correction Visual acuity less than 6/60 in the better eye (Option A ruled out): This level of visual acuity (or 20/200 in feet) is often referred to as legal blindness in many countries, including the United States, and is a criterion for eligibility for certain services. However, the international definition of blindness is typically more severe. Visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye after best possible correction (Option B): This is the definition of blindness according to the World Health Organization (WHO) and is widely adopted for international comparison. 3/60 means a person can see at 3 meters what a person with normal vision can see at 60 meters. This is the best definition of blindness among the choices. Visual field less than 10 degrees from fixation in the better eye (Option C ruled out): A restricted visual field can also define blindness, particularly "tunnel vision." The WHO definition of blindness includes "or corresponding visual field loss," which for blindness is typically a visual field of 10 degrees or less from fixation in the better eye. This is also a valid criterion for blindness. Inability to perceive light in both eyes(Option C ruled out): This is known as "No Light Perception" (NLP) and represents total blindness. While this is indeed a form of blindness, it is the most severe form. The general definition of "blindness" encompasses a broader range of severe visual impairment where some light perception or very limited vision might still be present. @Neet_pg_bot

However, the international definition of blindness is typically more severe.
 

Visual acuity less than 3/60 in the better eye after best possible correction (Option B): This is the definition of blindness according to the World Health Organization (WHO) and is widely adopted for international comparison. 3/60 means a person can see at 3 meters what a person with normal vision can see at 60 meters. This is the best definition of blindness among the choices.
 

Visual field less than 10 degrees from fixation in the better eye (Option C ruled out): A restricted visual field can also define blindness, particularly "tunnel vision." The WHO definition of blindness includes "or corresponding visual field loss," which for blindness is typically a visual field of 10 degrees or less from fixation in the better eye. This is also a valid criterion for blindness.
 

Inability to perceive light in both eyes(Option C ruled out): This is known as "No Light Perception" (NLP) and represents total blindness. While this is indeed a form of blindness, it is the most severe form. The general definition of "blindness" encompasses a broader range of severe visual impairment where some light perception or very limited vision might still be present.

questions.stem: Which of the following is one of the earliest presenting symptoms in a patient with Multiple Sclerosis?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is one of the earliest presenting symptoms in a patient with Multiple Sclerosis?
questions.solution: thesias (tingling, “pins and needles”), hypesthesia (numbness), and dysesthetic sensations (e.g., burning, swelling, tight wrapping) are among the most common and earliest symptoms in MS. They reflect demyelination in the sensory pathways and can appear abruptly or insidiously. Multiple sclerosis (MS) Clinical features: Abrupt or insidious onset of symptoms Sensory symptoms Paresthesias: tingling, prickling sensations, “pins and needles,” or painful burning. Hypesthesia: reduced sensation, numbness, or a “dead” feeling. Unpleasant sensations: feelings that body parts are swollen, wet, raw, or tightly wrapped. Pain is a common symptom of MS. Optic neuritis (ON) (Option C ruled out) Diminished visual acuity. Decreased colour perception in the central field of vision. May progress to severe visual loss. Periorbital pain. Fundoscopic examination: normal or optic disc swelling (papillitis), pallor of the optic disc (optic atrophy). Weakness of the limbs Loss of strength, speed, dexterity, and gait disturbance. Exercise-induced weakness is a characteristic symptom of MS. Upper motor neuron type weakness accompanied by other pyramidal signs. Facial weakness Lesion in the pons may resemble idiopathic Bell’s palsy. Spasticity Spontaneous and movement-induced muscle spasms. Painful spasms. Visual blurring Due to ON (optic neuritis) or diplopia. Diplopia is caused by internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) or palsy of the sixth cranial nerve. (Option D ruled out) Bilateral INO is particularly suggestive of MS. Other gaze disturbances in MS: Horizontal gaze palsy One-and-a-half syndrome (horizontal gaze palsy plus an INO) Acquired pendular nystagmus Ataxia Cerebellar tremors. Cerebellar dysarthria. Vertigo Lesion in the brainstem. Ancillary symptoms Paroxysmal symptoms Brief duration (10s to 2 min), high frequency (5–40 episodes per day), no change of consciousness or change in background electroencephalogram during episodes, and a self-limited course. Lhermitte’s symptom (Option A ruled out) An electric shock-like sensation that radiates down the back into the legs. Typically induced by flexion or other movements of the neck. Trigeminal neuralgia, hemifacial spasm, and glossopharyngeal neuralgia Demyelinating lesions involve the root entry or exit zone of the fifth, seventh, and ninth cranial nerve, respectively. Facial myokymia Persistent rapid flickering contractions of the facial musculature Slow spread of contraction across the face. Heat sensitivity Uthoff symptoms: Neurological symptoms develop from heat exposure, such as steam baths and saunas. Bladder dysfunction Present in >90% of MS patients. Detrusor hyperreflexia. Detrusor sphincter dyssynergia - hesitancy, urinary retention, overflow incontinence, and recurrent infection. Bowel dysfunction Constipation, faecal urgency or bowel incontinence. Cognitive dysfunction Memory loss. Impaired attention. Psychiatric symptom Depression. Fatigue 90% of patients experience fatigue. It causes work-related disability. Incorrect Options: Ataxia (Option B): Usually appears later due to cerebellar involvement, not a common early symptom. Vertigo (Option C): Caused by brainstem lesions, but not an early presenting symptom in MS. Facial palsy (Option D): Results from pontine lesions, but is rare as an initial symptom. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female with seizures was prescribed carbamazepine & erythromycin. A few days later, she developed ataxia. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.stemHtml: A 30-year-old female with seizures was prescribed carbamazepine & erythromycin. A few days later, she developed ataxia. What is the most likely cause of her symptoms?
questions.solution: he enzyme that metabolizes Carbamazepine , leading to elevated carbamazepine levels and resulting in toxicity, with ataxia being a common symptom. MOA: Inhibits high-frequency neuronal discharges and modulates voltage-gated sodium channels. Uses: Trigeminal neuralgia GTCS (generalized tonic clonic seizures) Partial seizures Bipolar disorder. Interactions: Metabolism of carbamazepine is induced by phenobarbitone, phenytoin, and vice versa. Erythromycin, fluoxetine, and isoniazid inhibit the metabolism of carbamazepine. (Option A) Adverse Effects Description Neurotoxicity Sedation, dizziness, vertigo, diplopia, and ataxia Gastrointestinal Effects Vomiting and diarrhoea occur with higher doses. Acute Intoxication Coma, convulsions, cardiovascular collapse. Haematological Agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia. Hypersensitivity Reactions Rashes, photosensitivity, hepatitis, lupus-like syndrome. Water Retention and Hyponatremia Due to enhanced antidiuretic hormone (ADH) action, it is more common in the elderly. Teratogenicity Increased incidence of minor fetal malformations. Incorrect Options: Erythromycin toxicity (Option B) is not the cause, as it rarely causes ataxia. Its main role here is as a CYP3A4 inhibitor, which increases carbamazepine levels and leads to toxicity. Worsening of the underlying disease (Option C) can cause ataxia, but the timing after starting erythromycin points to a drug interaction, making this less likely. A separate, unrelated neurological condition (Option D) is unlikely, as the timing with carbamazepine and erythromycin use suggests a drug interaction rather than a new, unrelated diagnosis. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
he enzyme that metabolizes Carbamazepine, leading to elevated carbamazepine levels and resulting in toxicity, with ataxia being a common symptom.
  • MOA: Inhibits high-frequency neuronal discharges and modulates voltage-gated sodium channels.
  • Uses:
    • Trigeminal neuralgia
    • GTCS (generalized tonic clonic seizures)
    • Partial seizures
    • Bipolar disorder.
  • Interactions:
    • Metabolism of carbamazepine is induced by phenobarbitone, phenytoin, and vice versa.
    • Erythromycin, fluoxetine, and isoniazid inhibit the metabolism of carbamazepine. (Option A)

Adverse Effects

Description

Neurotoxicity

Sedation, dizziness, vertigo, diplopia, and ataxia

Gastrointestinal Effects

Vomiting and diarrhoea occur with higher doses.

Acute Intoxication

Coma, convulsions, cardiovascular collapse.

Haematological

Agranulocytosis, aplastic anaemia.

Hypersensitivity Reactions

Rashes, photosensitivity, hepatitis, lupus-like syndrome.

Water Retention and Hyponatremia

Due to enhanced antidiuretic hormone (ADH) action, it is more common in the elderly.

Teratogenicity

Increased incidence of minor fetal malformations.

Incorrect Options:

Erythromycin toxicity (Option B) is not the cause, as it rarely causes ataxia. Its main role here is as a CYP3A4 inhibitor, which increases carbamazepine levels and leads to toxicity.

Worsening of the underlying disease (Option C) can cause ataxia, but the timing after starting erythromycin points to a drug interaction, making this less likely.

A separate, unrelated neurological condition (Option D) is unlikely, as the timing with carbamazepine and erythromycin use suggests a drug interaction rather than a new, unrelated diagnosis.

questions.stemHtml: A patient with schizophrenia says, "Hanuman ji is celibate. I am also celibate, so I am Hanuman." This statement is an example of:
questions.solution: tion: The given statement is a example of Austictic behaviour, as it is a illogical thinking, based entirely on the patient's inner mental world , disconnected from external logic or reality This is common in schizophrenia , where patients may draw bizarre and illogical conclusions that make sense only to them . According to Eugen Bleuler, the diagnostic criteria for schizophrenia include (4 ‘A’s): Affect (emotional expression) disturbances : Patients often exhibit diminished emotional expression, which can be observed through a lack of facial expressions and emotional responsiveness. Association (thought processes) disturbances: refers to disorganised thinking, where patients may form unusual or illogical connections in their thoughts, such as catastrophic beliefs about the world. Autism (social withdrawal) refers to detachment from reality, evident in patients who may appear silent around others and frequently engage in self-directed conversation. Ambivalence (mixed feelings) : Patients experience conflicting emotions or attitudes, which can lead to indecisiveness and difficulty making choices. Incorrect Options: Neologism (Option A) is creation of entirely new, made-up words or ordinary words used in a new way, are often linked to schizophrenia. Example: A patient says, "I need to go to the flibberflam store to get some boozleberries." These words are not real and have meaning only to the speaker. Word salad (Option B) is incoherent, incomprehensible mixture of words and phrases, often seen in advanced schizophrenia. ﻿﻿﻿Loosening of association (Option D) involves shifting from one idea to another with weak connections, but here the thoughts are tightly focused on one theme. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Which is the most common HPV serotype associated with cervical carcinoma?

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male presents with complaints of burning micturition. Prostatic examination was normal. Urinalysis shows >50 pus cells per high power field, but urine culture shows no growth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old male presents with complaints of burning micturition. Prostatic examination was normal. Urinalysis shows &gt;50 pus cells per high power field, but urine culture shows no growth. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Sterile pyuria is defined as the presence of >10 WBCs/mm³ or >3 WBCs/HPF in unspun urine, or a positive dipstick for leukocyte esterase/nitrites , without significant bacteriuria (i.e., <10⁵ CFU/mL on culture). It is the presence of pus cells in urine without bacterial growth on culture . It can result from non-bacterial infections (e.g., tuberculosis), inflammatory conditions , or prior antibiotic use. A normal prostate exam and no bacterial growth despite significant pyuria support this diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Chronic bacterial prostatitis (Option A): Typically shows positive urine culture and may have prostatic tenderness . Acute bacterial prostatitis (Option B): Presents with fever, painful prostate on DRE , and positive culture . Granulomatous prostatitis (Option C): Rare, often associated with tuberculosis , would show prostatic abnormalities . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A four-year-old child presents with difficulty in walking, a broad-based gait, and inability to perform heel-to-toe walking. The child was clingy towards his mother. On examination, the child is hyperreflexic and Babinski sign is positive. What could be the probable diagnosis ?
questions.stemHtml: A four-year-old child presents with difficulty in walking, a broad-based gait, and inability to perform heel-to-toe walking. The child was clingy towards his mother. On examination, the child is hyperreflexic and Babinski sign is positive. What could be the probable diagnosis ?
questions.solution: p>The child’s chronic spasticity, hyperreflexia, and gait abnormalities align with Cerebral Palsy, a static motor disorder due to early brain injury. The absence of acute-onset or sensory deficits rules out GBS, ADEM, or spinal cord lesions. Motor Symptoms: Difficulty walking, broad-based gait, and inability to perform heel-to-toe walking are classic signs of spastic diplegia, a common form of CP. Spastic diplegia primarily affects the lower limbs, leading to gait disturbances. Hyperreflexia and a positive Babinski sign indicate upper motor neuron (UMN) involvement, which is characteristic of CP. Age and Development: CP is a non-progressive disorder caused by early brain injury (prenatal, perinatal, or postnatal). Symptoms typically manifest in early childhood, as seen in this 4-year-old. Behavioral Observation: The child being clingy may reflect associated behavioral or cognitive impairments, which are common in CP. Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) ( Option A ) GBS presents with areflexia and ascending paralysis, not hyperreflexia or spasticity. It is also acute-onset, unlike CP. ADEM ( Option C ) ADEM is a post-infectious demyelinating disorder with acute-onset encephalopathy (e.g., seizures, mental status changes), not a chronic gait disorder. Spinal cord lesion ( Option D ) While spinal cord lesions can cause UMN signs, they are typically acquired (e.g., trauma, tumor) and would not explain the chronic, non-progressive nature of CP. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient presents with low back pain. Bone scan reveals the characteristic "Honda H" sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A patient presents with low back pain. Bone scan reveals the characteristic "Honda H" sign. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: y fracture Explanation: The “Honda H” sign on a Bone scan refers to a specific pattern of fracture lines seen in the sacrum, which is suggestive of Bilateral sacral insufficiency fractures. Bilateral sacral insufficiency fractures typically occur in elderly patients or those with osteoporosis , chronic steroid use, or other metabolic bone diseases. It can also happen in patients with Rheumatoid arthritis. These fractures are caused by normal or physiological stress on weakened bone . Acute osteomyelitis (Option A) would typically show localized bone marrow edema with possible abscess formation but does not produce the “Honda H” sign. Marrow edema (Option B) is a non-specific finding that can result from trauma, infection, or inflammation but lacks the specific fracture pattern of the “Honda H” sign. Metastatic sacral lesion (Option D) usually appears as destructive or infiltrative lesions on MRI, not the bilateral linear fracture pattern of the “Honda H” sign. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with hepatosplenomegaly and cherry-red spots on the retina. The child exhibits a normal startle reflex but shows developmental regression. Based on these clinical features, which of the following enzymes is deficient in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 5-year-old child presents with hepatosplenomegaly and cherry-red spots on the retina. The child exhibits a normal startle reflex but shows developmental regression. Based on these clinical features, which of the following enzymes is deficient in this patient?
questions.solution: Hexosaminidase A (Deficient in Tay-Sachs disease): (Option A ruled out) Features: Cherry-red spot, developmental regression, exaggerated startle reflex (hyperacusis), progressive neurodegeneration, no hepatosplenomegaly. Fit with case: The presence of hepatosplenomegaly and normal startle reflex rules out classic Tay-Sachs. Sphingomyelinase (Deficient in Niemann-Pick disease Types A and B): (Option B) Features: Hepatosplenomegaly, developmental regression (especially in Type A), cherry-red spots (in Type A), interstitial lung disease, foam cells in bone marrow. The startle reflex is typically normal or not exaggerated. Fit with case: This aligns very well with all the described symptoms: hepatosplenomegaly, cherry-red spots, developmental regression, and a normal startle reflex. Niemann-Pick Type A is the severe neurovisceral form. Glucocerebrosidase (Deficient in Gaucher disease): (Option C ruled out) Features: Hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises, pancytopenia, varying neurological involvement (Type 2 has severe neurodegeneration, Type 1 is non-neuropathic, Type 3 has progressive neurological features). Cherry-red spots are rare or absent. Fit with case: The presence of cherry-red spots makes Gaucher disease less likely. Arylsulfatase A (Deficient in Metachromatic Leukodystrophy): (Option D ruled out) Features: Progressive demyelination leading to neurological symptoms (ataxia, spasticity, regression), peripheral neuropathy. Hepatosplenomegaly and cherry-red spots are typically absent. Fit with case: This does not fit the hepatosplenomegaly or cherry-red spot findings. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 20-year-old female diagnosed with septic shock presents with a blood pressure of 58/630 mmHg. After receiving 30 ml/kg of crystalloid fluid, her mean arterial pressure (MAP) remains 58 mmHg. What is the next best step in management?
questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old female diagnosed with septic shock presents with a blood pressure of 58/630 mmHg. After receiving 30 ml/kg of crystalloid fluid, her mean arterial pressure (MAP) remains 58 mmHg. What is the next best step in management?
questions.solution: rong>Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) is the vasopressor of choice in septic shock due to its potent alpha-1 effects (vasoconstriction) and minimal beta effects, improving MAP without excessive tachycardia. Septic Shock Management: 1. Source Control Start broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour. Remove infected/ necrotic tissue or devices if they are the source. 2. Shock Management (within 6 hours) Fluids: Crystalloids (NS/albumin) up to 80 mL/kg. Target: CVP 8–12 mmHg, MAP ≥65 mmHg, ScvO₂ ≥70%. Use norepinephrine (warm shock) or epinephrine (cold shock) as first-line vasopressors if fluid therapy fails. Dopamine is no longer preferred due to adverse hormonal effects. 3. Enhancing Host Response Steroids if shock is vasopressor-refractory or cortisol is low. Vasopressin can be added in refractory shock. Drug of Choice in Shock: Anaphylactic shock: Adrenaline. Cardiogenic shock: Noradrenaline or dopamine. Distributive shock: Noradrenaline or phenylephrine. Hypovolemic shock: Crystalloids or fluids. Secondary shock: Prazosin. Shock with oliguria: Dopamine. Hypoadrenal shock: Corticosteroids. Septic shock: Broad-spectrum antibiotics, Noradrenaline. Incorrect Options: Start dopamine (Option A): Less preferred due to higher risk of arrhythmias and worse outcomes compared to noradrenaline. Repeat crystalloid fluid (Option C): Already received appropriate volume; additional fluid may cause fluid overload without improving perfusion. Start vasopressin (Option D): Vasopressin is used as an adjunct to noradrenaline in refractory cases, not as initial therapy. @Neet_pg_bot

rong>Noradrenaline (norepinephrine) is the vasopressor of choice in septic shock due to its potent alpha-1 effects (vasoconstriction) and minimal beta effects, improving MAP without excessive tachycardia.

Septic Shock Management:

1. Source Control

  • Start broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour.
    Remove infected/ necrotic tissue or devices if they are the source.

2. Shock Management (within 6 hours)

  • Fluids: Crystalloids (NS/albumin) up to 80 mL/kg.
  • Target: CVP 8–12 mmHg, MAP ≥65 mmHg, ScvO₂ ≥70%.
  • Use norepinephrine (warm shock) or epinephrine (cold shock) as first-line vasopressors if fluid therapy fails.
  • Dopamine is no longer preferred due to adverse hormonal effects.

3. Enhancing Host Response

  • Steroids if shock is vasopressor-refractory or cortisol is low.
  • Vasopressin can be added in refractory shock.

Drug of Choice in Shock:

  • Anaphylactic shock: Adrenaline.
  • Cardiogenic shock: Noradrenaline or dopamine.
  • Distributive shock: Noradrenaline or phenylephrine.
  • Hypovolemic shock: Crystalloids or fluids.
  • Secondary shock: Prazosin.
  • Shock with oliguria: Dopamine.
  • Hypoadrenal shock: Corticosteroids.
  • Septic shock: Broad-spectrum antibiotics, Noradrenaline.

Incorrect Options:

Start dopamine (Option A): Less preferred due to higher risk of arrhythmias and worse outcomes compared to noradrenaline.

Repeat crystalloid fluid (Option C): Already received appropriate volume; additional fluid may cause fluid overload without improving perfusion.

Start vasopressin (Option D): Vasopressin is used as an adjunct to noradrenaline in refractory cases, not as initial therapy.

questions.stem: A 20-year-old male presents with severe headache, vomiting & photophobia. On examination, neck rigidity and Brudzinski's sign are positive. A CT scan of the brain shows hydrocephalus and no haemorrhage. CSF examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 20-year-old male presents with severe headache, vomiting & photophobia. On examination, neck rigidity and Brudzinski's sign are positive. A CT scan of the brain shows hydrocephalus and no haemorrhage. CSF examination is normal. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: ong>Explanation: SAH often presents with sudden severe headache, vomiting, photophobia, and meningeal signs. CT may miss early or small bleeds, and CSF can be normal if bleeding is minimal or delayed. Hydrocephalus suggests impaired CSF drainage due to subarachnoid blood. Subarachnoid hemorrhage Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH): Blood accumulation in the subarachnoid space. Causes: Often due to aneurysm rupture (~85%) or trauma . Non-traumatic SAH is most commonly caused by the rupture of a saccular aneurysm . Clinical Impact: High mortality and morbidity; often presents with a sudden, severe headache (worst headache of life). Complications: Seizures, vasospasm, hydrocephalus, and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI). Epidemiology: Age/ Gender: Most of the SAH occurs between age of 40-60, mean rupture age 50-55 and slightly more prevalent in females. Risk Factors: Smoking and history of ruptured aneurysms increase SAH risk. Etiology: Aneurysmal SAH (aSAH): Risk Factors: Hypertension , smoking , family history, alcohol use, sympathomimetic drugs , and estrogen deficiency . Rupture Risk: (Option D) Age >60 Posterior circulation aneurysms Atherosclerosis Aneurysm size Aneurysms <10 mm: ~0.1% annual rupture risk. Aneurysms ≥10 mm: 0.5–1% annual rupture risk. Giant aneurysms (>2.5 cm): ~6% rupture risk in first year. Family history Previous SAH ADPKD Nonaneurysmal SAH (NASAH): Perimesencephalic NASAH : Localized blood in perimesencephalic cisterns, normal angiography, benign course. Occult Aneurysm : Small aneurysms missed on initial angiography, detectable on repeat imaging. Vascular Malformations: Includes arteriovenous malformations (AVM) and dural arteriovenous fistulae. Treated with surgery or endovascular interventions. Intracranial Arterial Dissection: Diagnosed by angiography, causes severe bleeding, treated with surgery or endovascular methods. Other Causes: Cocaine abuse, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, cerebral venous thrombosis, sickle cell disorders, moyamoya disease, cerebral vasculitis, bleeding disorders. Pathophysiology: Hemodynamic Stress : Central to intracranial aneurysm formation, especially at arterial bifurcations. Aneurysm Rupture: Causes neurological damage through compression of adjacent brain tissue and ischemia from reduced blood flow. Mechanisms: Hemodynamic stress and inflammation (matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-mediated degradation of extracellular matrix) weaken the arterial wall, promoting aneurysm formation and rupture. Inflammatory Response: Macrophages and smooth muscle cells drive these degenerative processes. Clinical features: Sudden, severe "thunderclap" headache (hallmark) Loss of consciousness: Increase in intracranial pressure. It presses the reticular activating system. Leads to the development of stupor and coma. Worst headache of the life Nuchal rigidity is due to blood but no fever. Vomiting Sentinel bleed: microbleeds from the berry Aneurysm Investigations: Non-contrast CT head: "Hyperdense" blood in the subarachnoid space ("SAH star") Lumbar puncture: Xanthochromia (yellowish discoloration) of CSF after 12 hours Cerebral angiography: Identifies aneurysms or AVMs CT angiography or MR angiography: Non-invasive methods to detect vascular abnormalities Incorrect Options: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus (NPH) (Option A): Presents with triad: dementia, gait disturbance, urinary incontinence—not acute meningeal symptoms. Bacterial Meningitis (Option B): Would show abnormal CSF: high protein, low glucose, and neutrophilic pleocytosis. Viral Encephalitis (Option C): Presents with altered sensorium, seizures, and abnormal CSF (lymphocytic pleocytosis), not just headache and normal CSF. @Neet_pg_bot

ong>Explanation:
  • SAH often presents with sudden severe headache, vomiting, photophobia, and meningeal signs. CT may miss early or small bleeds, and CSF can be normal if bleeding is minimal or delayed. Hydrocephalus suggests impaired CSF drainage due to subarachnoid blood.

Subarachnoid hemorrhage
  • Subarachnoid Hemorrhage (SAH): Blood accumulation in the subarachnoid space.
  • Causes: Often due to aneurysm rupture (~85%) or trauma.
  • Non-traumatic SAH is most commonly caused by the rupture of a saccular aneurysm.
  • Clinical Impact: High mortality and morbidity; often presents with a sudden, severe headache (worst headache of life).
  • Complications: Seizures, vasospasm, hydrocephalus, and delayed cerebral ischemia (DCI).

Epidemiology:

  • Age/ Gender: Most of the SAH occurs between age of 40-60, mean rupture age 50-55 and slightly more prevalent in females.
  • Risk Factors: Smoking and history of ruptured aneurysms increase SAH risk.

Etiology:

  • Aneurysmal SAH (aSAH):
    • Risk Factors: Hypertension, smoking, family history, alcohol use, sympathomimetic drugs, and estrogen deficiency.
    • Rupture Risk: (Option D)
      • Age >60
      • Posterior circulation aneurysms
      • Atherosclerosis
      • Aneurysm size
        • Aneurysms <10 mm: ~0.1% annual rupture risk.
        • Aneurysms ≥10 mm: 0.5–1% annual rupture risk.
        • Giant aneurysms (>2.5 cm): ~6% rupture risk in first year.
      • Family history
      • Previous SAH
      • ADPKD
  • Nonaneurysmal SAH (NASAH):
    • Perimesencephalic NASAH: Localized blood in perimesencephalic cisterns, normal angiography, benign course.
    • Occult Aneurysm: Small aneurysms missed on initial angiography, detectable on repeat imaging.
    • Vascular Malformations: Includes arteriovenous malformations (AVM) and dural arteriovenous fistulae. Treated with surgery or endovascular interventions.
    • Intracranial Arterial Dissection: Diagnosed by angiography, causes severe bleeding, treated with surgery or endovascular methods.
    • Other Causes: Cocaine abuse, cerebral amyloid angiopathy, cerebral venous thrombosis, sickle cell disorders, moyamoya disease, cerebral vasculitis, bleeding disorders.

Pathophysiology:

  • Hemodynamic Stress: Central to intracranial aneurysm formation, especially at arterial bifurcations.
  • Aneurysm Rupture: Causes neurological damage through compression of adjacent brain tissue and ischemia from reduced blood flow.
    • Mechanisms: Hemodynamic stress and inflammation (matrix metalloproteinase (MMP)-mediated degradation of extracellular matrix) weaken the arterial wall, promoting aneurysm formation and rupture.
    • Inflammatory Response: Macrophages and smooth muscle cells drive these degenerative processes.

Clinical features:

  • Sudden, severe "thunderclap" headache (hallmark)
  • Loss of consciousness: Increase in intracranial pressure.
    • It presses the reticular activating system.
    • Leads to the development of stupor and coma.
  • Worst headache of the life
  • Nuchal rigidity is due to blood but no fever.
  • Vomiting
  • Sentinel bleed: microbleeds from the berry Aneurysm

Investigations:

  • Non-contrast CT head: "Hyperdense" blood in the subarachnoid space ("SAH star")
  • Lumbar puncture: Xanthochromia (yellowish discoloration) of CSF after 12 hours
  • Cerebral angiography: Identifies aneurysms or AVMs
  • CT angiography or MR angiography: Non-invasive methods to detect vascular abnormalities

Incorrect Options:

questions.stem: Ascent to high altitude causes ?
questions.stemHtml: Ascent to high altitude causes ?
questions.solution: >alkalosis Explanation: At high altitudes, hypoxia triggers hyperventilation, leading to enhanced CO₂ removal and results in respiratory alkalosis. Changes during Acclimatization Respiratory At high altitudes, lower oxygen levels stimulate peripheral chemoreceptors, increasing pulmonary ventilation. This leads to enhanced CO2 removal, causing respiratory alkalosis. Kidneys respond by excreting more bicarbonate to stabilize blood pH, causing a sustained increase in ventilation and supporting prolonged acclimatization. Haematological At high altitudes, lower PO2 boosts erythropoietin production, increasing red blood cell count. This also raises 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) levels in red blood cells. Initially, alkalosis shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the left but increased 2,3-DPG shifts it to the right, improving oxygen release to tissues. Cardiovascular Hypoxia activates the sympathoadrenal axis, increasing heart rate, cardiac output, and blood pressure. Increased cardiac output leads to an increase in blood flow, and hypoxia causes vasodilation in the systemic circulation, further contributing to increased blood flow and oxygen supply to the tissues. Tissue In acclimatization, skeletal muscles undergo several changes, including an increase in the number of capillaries and mitochondria and an increase in myoglobin content. Further, chemicals released from the hypoxic tissues stimulate angiogenesis. Metabolic acidosis (Option A) involves decreased bicarbonate levels due to conditions like diarrhea or renal failure, not high altitude. Metabolic alkalosis (Option B) can occur later as a compensatory renal response to respiratory alkalosis but is not the initial effect. Respiratory acidosis (Option C) results from hypoventilation and CO₂ retention . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: ul> Internal Laryngeal Nerve (ILN) (Option A): The internal laryngeal nerve is a branch of the superior laryngeal nerve (which in turn is a branch of the vagus nerve). External Laryngeal Nerve (ELN) (Option B ruled out): The external laryngeal nerve is primarily motor, supplying the cricothyroid muscle (which tenses the vocal cords). questions.stem: Tight junctions are primarily located at which part of the cell?

questions.solution: Correct answers- a) Apical Tight Junctions (Zonula Occludens): Structure: Sealing strands of transmembrane adhesion proteins (Occludin, Claudins, JAMs) that directly join to occlude intercellular space. Location: Primarily at the apical (Option A) margins of epithelial and endothelial cells, forming a continuous belt. NOT in connective tissue. Function: Limit/regulate permeability of epithelial cells to ions and solutes (prevent leakage via paracellular pathway). Essential for endothelial barrier function and vasodilation. Permeability: While primarily seals, they can permit selective passage of some ions/small molecules via controlled paracellular channels, not free passage. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: Arrange the steps for the pap smear.
questions.solution: ng a Pap Smear are as follows: Position the patient in the lithotomy position Perform a per speculum (PS) examination Collect the cervical sample Site Transformation zone of the cervix, where the squamous epithelium (ectocervix) and columnar epithelium (endocervix) meet. This is the most common site for cervical cancer to develop. Instruments Ayre spatula collects cells from the ectocervix Cervical broom (also called a cytobrush) from transition zone Endocervical brush from endocervix Procedure Steps: (Option A) The Pap smear should be obtained before vaginal examination. The fingers may remove desquamated cervical cells and give a false-negative report Lubricant may prevent detection of organisms Vaginal bleeding during examination may preclude a proper visualization of the cervix. The patient should not have intercourse or touch for 24 hours before test. The patient is placed in the lithotomyl position, with the labia parted Speculum is gently introduced without the use of lubricant or jelly. The squamocolumnar junction is now scraped with Ayre's spatula by rotating the spatula all around. Conventional Pap smear : Cells are collected with a spatula or brush, smeared onto a slide, and immediately fixed with a spray fixative or by immersing in 95% ethanol with/without ether Liquid-based cytology : Cells are collected and then rinsed into a liquid fixative vial. This is considered more sensitive than the conventional Pap smear as it provides a more uniform distribution of cells. Indications Cervical cancer screening : Routine screening for women aged 21-65 years, with the frequency and type of testing varying based on age and risk factors. Evaluation of abnormal vaginal bleeding : While not a primary diagnostic tool, a Pap smear is performed as part of the workup, along with other tests. Timing & Frequency Age 21-29: Cytology (Pap smear) every 3 years. Age 30-65: Co-testing (Pap smear + HPV testing) every 5 years. >65: No further screening if they have had 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative co-test results and no history of high-grade precancerous lesions. H/o of CIN 2 or higher: Annual screening for 20 years. More frequent screening in HIV and Immunocompromised patients. C/I Avoid during menstruation (Relative Contraindication). @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
ng a Pap Smear are as follows:
  • Position the patient in the lithotomy position
  • Perform a per speculum (PS) examination
  • Collect the cervical sample

Site
  • Transformation zone of the cervix, where the squamous epithelium (ectocervix) and columnar epithelium (endocervix) meet.
  • This is the most common site for cervical cancer to develop.

Instruments
  • Ayre spatula collects cells from the ectocervix
  • Cervical broom (also called a cytobrush) from transition zone
  • Endocervical brush from endocervix

Procedure
  • Steps: (Option A)
    • The Pap smear should be obtained before vaginal examination.
      • The fingers may remove desquamated cervical cells and give a false-negative report
      • Lubricant may prevent detection of organisms
      • Vaginal bleeding during examination may preclude a proper visualization of the cervix.
    • The patient should not have intercourse or touch for 24 hours before test.
    • The patient is placed in the lithotomyl position, with the labia parted
    • Speculum is gently introduced without the use of lubricant or jelly.
    • The squamocolumnar junction is now scraped with Ayre's spatula by rotating the spatula all around.
  • Conventional Pap smear: Cells are collected with a spatula or brush, smeared onto a slide, and immediately fixed with a spray fixative or by immersing in 95% ethanol with/without ether
  • Liquid-based cytology: Cells are collected and then rinsed into a liquid fixative vial. This is considered more sensitive than the conventional Pap smear as it provides a more uniform distribution of cells.

Indications
  • Cervical cancer screening: Routine screening for women aged 21-65 years, with the frequency and type of testing varying based on age and risk factors.
  • Evaluation of abnormal vaginal bleeding: While not a primary diagnostic tool, a Pap smear is performed as part of the workup, along with other tests.

Timing & Frequency
  • Age 21-29: Cytology (Pap smear) every 3 years.
  • Age 30-65: Co-testing (Pap smear + HPV testing) every 5 years.
  • >65: No further screening if they have had 3 consecutive negative cytology results or 2 consecutive negative co-test results and no history of high-grade precancerous lesions.
  • H/o of CIN 2 or higher: Annual screening for 20 years.
  • More frequent screening in HIV and Immunocompromised patients.

C/I

Avoid during menstruation (Relative Contraindication).

rong>Explanation

1. Plain Radiographs (X-rays):

  • Often Normal: Plain X-rays are notoriously insensitive for detecting acute sacral insufficiency fractures, especially in the early stages. The subtle nature of the fracture and overlying bowel gas can obscure them.
  • Subtle Sclerosis: In later stages or chronic cases, a vague vertical band of increased bone density (sclerosis) may be noted in the sacral ala (wing) parallel to the sacroiliac joint. This represents healing bone or callus formation.

2. Bone Scintigraphy (Nuclear Medicine Bone Scan):

  • Highly Sensitive: Bone scans (using technetium-99m methylene diphosphonate, 99mTc-MDP) are very sensitive for detecting SIFs, often showing uptake earlier than other modalities.
  • "H-Sign" or "Honda Sign": This is a classic and highly characteristic finding, though not present in all cases (occurs in 20-78% of cases). It refers to a pattern of increased radionuclide uptake resembling the letter "H".

3. Computed Tomography (CT Scan):

  • Better for Bony Detail: CT is superior to plain X-rays for visualizing subtle cortical breaks and fracture lines.
  • Fracture Line: A low-attenuation (dark) fracture line may be seen, often with surrounding ill-defined sclerosis representing callus formation.
  • Sclerosis: Broad regions of sclerosis adjacent to the fracture line can be present.

questions.stem: What is the treatment of choice for complicated gonorrhea caused by penicillin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae?
questions.stemHtml: What is the treatment of choice for complicated gonorrhea caused by penicillin-resistant Neisseria gonorrhoeae?
questions.solution: roducing organisms. Neisseria Gonorrhoeae: Clinical Features Men Urethritis, purulent urethral discharge, dysuria, epididymitis, prostatitis. Women Cervicitis, vaginal discharge, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), dysuria, and intermenstrual bleeding. Rarely can cause Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome. Pharyngeal Infection Often asymptomatic, sore throat, pharyngitis. Rectal Infection Proctitis, rectal discharge, pain, and tenesmus, may be asymptomatic. Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI) Fever, dermatitis, polyarthralgia, septic arthritis. Neonates Ophthalmia neonatorum, conjunctivitis, potential for blindness if untreated. Diagnosis Gram Stain Gram-negative diplococci within polymorphonuclear leukocytes (particularly useful in men). Culture Thayer-Martin or other selective media, oxidase-positive, and carbohydrate utilization tests. NAAT (Nucleic Acid Amplification Test) Highly sensitive and specific, recommended for urogenital, pharyngeal, and rectal specimens. Serological Tests Not commonly used due to lower sensitivity and specificity compared to NAAT and culture. Treatment- Green STD kit First-Line Therapy Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM as a single dose PLUS doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days (if chlamydial co-infection is not excluded). (Option A) Alternative Therapy Gentamicin 240 mg IM as a single dose PLUS azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose (if ceftriaxone is not available). Amoxicillin (Option B) is a beta-lactam antibiotic from the penicillin class. Once used for gonorrhea, it is now largely ineffective due to widespread resistance from penicillinase-producing N. gonorrhoeae strains. Cross-resistance with penicillin makes it an unreliable treatment option. Tetracycline (Option C) , once used for gonorrhea, is now ineffective due to widespread resistance in N. gonorrhoeae. Its reduced efficacy makes it unsuitable as monotherapy and it no longer meets current treatment standards. Neisseria Gonorrhoeae:

Clinical Features

Men

Urethritis, purulent urethral discharge, dysuria, epididymitis, prostatitis.

Women

Cervicitis, vaginal discharge, pelvic inflammatory disease (PID), dysuria, and intermenstrual bleeding.

Rarely can cause Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome.

Pharyngeal Infection

Often asymptomatic, sore throat, pharyngitis.

Rectal Infection

Proctitis, rectal discharge, pain, and tenesmus, may be asymptomatic.

Disseminated Gonococcal Infection (DGI)

Fever, dermatitis, polyarthralgia, septic arthritis.

Neonates

Ophthalmia neonatorum, conjunctivitis, potential for blindness if untreated.

Diagnosis

Gram Stain

Gram-negative diplococci within polymorphonuclear leukocytes (particularly useful in men).

Culture

Thayer-Martin or other selective media, oxidase-positive, and carbohydrate utilization tests.

NAAT (Nucleic Acid Amplification Test)

Highly sensitive and specific, recommended for urogenital, pharyngeal, and rectal specimens.

Serological Tests

Not commonly used due to lower sensitivity and specificity compared to NAAT and culture.

Treatment- Green STD kit

Ceftriaxone 500 mg IM as a single dose PLUS doxycycline 100 mg orally twice daily for 7 days (if chlamydial co-infection is not excluded). (Option A)

Alternative Therapy

Gentamicin 240 mg IM as a single dose PLUS azithromycin 2 g orally as a single dose (if ceftriaxone is not available).

Amoxicillin (Option B) is a beta-lactam antibiotic from the penicillin class. Once used for gonorrhea, it is now largely ineffective due to widespread resistance from penicillinase-producing N. gonorrhoeae strains. Cross-resistance with penicillin makes it an unreliable treatment option.

Tetracycline (Option C), once used for gonorrhea, is now ineffective due to widespread resistance in N. gonorrhoeae. Its reduced efficacy makes it unsuitable as monotherapy and it no longer meets current treatment standards.

questions.stem: Which one of the following cranial nerves is not involved in olfaction ?
questions.stemHtml: Which one of the following cranial nerves is not involved in olfaction ?
questions.solution: nerve is a purely a motor nerve supplying muscles of the tongue and has no sensory or olfactory role. It innervates all the tongue muscles (intrinsic and extrinsic) except for the palatoglossus, which receives motor innervation from the vagal nerve (CN X). The muscular/lingual branch is a general somatic efferent (GSE) which controls most tongue actions, including protruding, retracting, depressing the tongue, and changing the tongue’s shape. Olfaction (sense of smell) is primarily carried by Cranial Nerve I (Olfactory Nerve). However, cranial nerves V (Trigeminal) (Option D) , VII (Facial) , IX (Glossopharyngeal) (Option C) , and X (Vagus) (Option B) are involved in detecting irritating or pungent odors , contributing to reflex responses like sneezing or coughing. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: B

options.label: C

questions.answerText: Increased lactate is produced even in the presence of oxygen
questions.solution: cells exhibit a phenomenon known as the Warburg effect, where they consume more glucose and convert it to lactate even when oxygen is plentiful (aerobic glycolysis). This process allows cancer cells to generate energy and biosynthetic precursors rapidly to support their uncontrolled growth, despite the inefficiency of producing only 2 ATPs per glucose molecule compared to the 36-38 ATPs from oxidative phosphorylation in normal cells. Increased GLUT-2 transporters, oxidative phosphorylation (Option A) - While increased glucose uptake via GLUT transporters is a feature of cancer cells, oxidative phosphorylation is reduced in cancer cells due to the Warburg effect. They rely more on glycolysis and lactate production rather than oxidative phosphorylation. Increased conversion of pyruvate to Acetyl CoA (Option B) - In normal cells, pyruvate is converted to Acetyl CoA for entry into the citric acid cycle under aerobic conditions. However, in cancer cells, pyruvate is preferentially converted to lactate due to the Warburg effect, not to Acetyl CoA. Increased fatty acid oxidation (Option D) - Fatty acid oxidation is more characteristic of normal cells or certain cancer types under specific conditions, but it is not the primary process for increased glucose consumption in cancer cells. @Neet_pg_bot
